provenance.hash_method: Artifact, manifest and catalog hashes cover actual input-file bytes. Rule hashes cover UTF-8 JSON.stringify(rule) with its original parsed property order; selected rule objects are unchanged.
limitations: Selection reasons are supplied explicitly by the operator; this script does not perform or certify legal review.
Only the named rules are selected, from one named artifact per source. Unselected candidates and alternative runs are not silently merged.
Source-level review items and no-rule findings remain separate from selected rules; their presence does not mean that every selected rule is executable or that every source issue was resolved.
Coverage prose awaiting execution review stays non-executable. Missing facts and uncertain legal interpretation are not resolved by selection.
This intermediate file does not replace or modify the public rule pack or submission exports. Downstream assembly must preserve the recorded rule hashes and origin.

rules.title: Initial rent limit after voluntary vacancy
rules.requirement: For qualifying vacancy decontrol after a tenant voluntarily vacates, the landlord must limit the new tenant's initial rent increase to 25% over the prior tenant's last rent, excluding any capital improvement surcharge from that prior rent.
rules.key_value: 25% above prior rent, excluding capital improvement surcharge
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a landlord setting a new tenant's initial rent under Article VII for a residential apartment in a dwelling registered in accordance with § 155-30, after the prior tenant voluntarily vacates without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or the landlord's agents. The unit may not be decontrolled more than once in any three-year period. This finding addresses the expressly described voluntary-vacancy calculation; application of that calculation after eviction requires review.
rules.exemptions: Any capital improvement surcharge included in the prior tenant's last rent is excluded from the comparison amount.
rules.quoted_span: Provided that a dwelling is registered in accordance with § 155-30 upon the vacation of a residential apartment unit by a tenant, the apartment unit shall become decontrolled and exempt from the provisions of this chapter for the new tenant's initial rental; provided, however, that said rental shall be limited to an increase of 25% over the last rental paid by the tenant who voluntarily vacated the rental unit, exclusive of any capital improvement surcharge that is a component of said last rental.

rules.title: Subsequent increases and new base rent
rules.requirement: After the new tenant's initial rent under vacancy decontrol, additional rent increases must comply with Chapter 155. Computations under that chapter must use the initial base rent charged to the new tenant under § 155-31 as the base rent.
rules.key_value: Initial rent becomes the base rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords imposing additional increases, and computations under Chapter 155, after a new tenant receives an initial rent under Article VII vacancy decontrol of a residential apartment in a dwelling registered under § 155-30. Qualifying vacancy circumstances are voluntary departure without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or departure resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground is unavailable for dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Decontrol is limited to once in any three-year period. Disputed vacancy circumstances are determined by the Rent Control Board after a hearing.
rules.exemptions: The Article VII exemption is limited to the new tenant's initial rent.
rules.quoted_span: However, any additional rental increase beyond the initial rental of the new tenant shall be subject to the provisions of this chapter. For the purpose of any computations under this chapter, the initial base rent charged to the new tenant under this section shall be considered the base rent.

rules.title: Permitted vacancy circumstances and improper decontrol remedies
rules.requirement: A landlord may claim Article VII decontrol only for voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground excludes dispossession based on holding over after the tenant's term expires. The Rent Control Board decides disputed vacancy circumstances after a hearing and, if it finds a landlord seeking or having obtained decontrol after a vacancy outside the permitted circumstances, may rescind decontrol, with rent reverting to its pre-vacancy amount, and prosecute the landlord under § 155-21.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords seeking or having obtained Article VII vacancy decontrol of residential apartment units. Article VII requires dwelling registration under § 155-30 and permits decontrol no more than once in any three-year period. Permitted vacancy grounds are voluntary departure without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or the landlord's agents, legal eviction, or departure resulting from an order of a court of competent jurisdiction; the court-order ground is unavailable to a landlord receiving a dispossession order based on the tenant holding over after expiration of the term. The stated remedies require a Board finding that the tenant vacated under circumstances outside § 155-32.
rules.exemptions: The court-order ground does not include dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord shall be entitled to decontrol the apartment unit under this article only under the following circumstances:

A.

If the tenant vacates the apartment voluntarily without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or his agents or if the tenant is legally evicted.

B.
If the tenant vacates the apartment as a result of a court order from a court of competent jurisdiction. This ground shall not be available to a landlord who receives a court order to dispossess a tenant based upon the tenant holding over and continuing in possession of the premises after the expiration of his term. Whenever there is an issue as to the circumstances under which a tenant has vacated an apartment unit, that issue shall be determined by the Rent Control Board after a hearing.
If the Board finds that a landlord is seeking to decontrol or has decontrolled an apartment unit and the tenant has vacated the unit under circumstances other than those set forth in this section, the Rent Board may rescind the decontrol of the apartment unit, and the rent shall revert to that rental on the apartment unit prior to the vacation of the apartment, and prosecute the landlord for violation of the chapter under § 155-21 .

rules.title: Vacancy decontrol certificate and filing fee
rules.requirement: When an apartment is decontrolled under Article VII, the landlord must file the Rent Leveling Board's certificate with a $50 filing fee. The certificate must identify the vacating tenant, existing rent, circumstances of vacancy, new tenant, new rent and effective date of the new rent.
rules.key_value: $50 certificate filing fee
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to the landlord whenever an apartment unit is decontrolled under Article VII. Authorized decontrol concerns a residential apartment in a dwelling registered under § 155-30, following voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground excludes dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Decontrol is limited to once in any three-year period, and disputed vacancy circumstances are decided by the Rent Control Board after a hearing. The filing trigger is decontrol under Article VII, not a tenant's application for housing.
rules.quoted_span: When any apartment unit is decontrolled under this article, the landlord shall file a certificate, provided by the Rent Leveling Board, including a filing fee in the amount of $50, indicating the name of the vacating tenant, the existing rental, the circumstances under which the tenant vacated the apartment unit, the name of the new tenant, the new rental and the effective date of the new rental.

rules.title: Decontrol limited to once in three years
rules.requirement: A landlord may not decontrol a dwelling unit under Article VII more than once in any three-year period.
rules.key_value: Once in any three-year period
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords seeking Article VII vacancy decontrol of dwelling units. Article VII concerns residential apartments in dwellings registered under § 155-30 and requires voluntary vacancy without landlord or agent harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure, legal eviction, or vacancy resulting from a competent court's order; the court-order ground is unavailable for dispossession based on holding over after expiration of the tenant's term. Disputed vacancy circumstances are decided by the Rent Control Board after a hearing. The frequency restriction concerns decontrol under this article.
rules.quoted_span: No dwelling unit shall be decontrolled pursuant to this article more than once in any three-year period.

rules.title: Residential rental application fee limit
rules.requirement: A covered landlord or landlord's agent must not require an application or similar fee exceeding $50 to apply to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Violators face penalties of up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second offense, and $1,000 for each subsequent offense, enforced through summary proceedings in the property's county Superior Court, Law Division, Special Civil Part upon a complaint by the Division of Consumer Affairs Director or Attorney General; following proceedings, the amount wrongfully charged must be remitted to the applicant or prospective tenant from the collected penalty.
rules.key_value: $50 as of 2026-10-01; subject to statutory annual adjustment
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units located in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent are exempt. New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees are exempt unless they are the landlord of the residential rental property.
rules.quoted_span:
1. a. A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
b.  A landlord, or agent thereof, who violates
subsection a. of this section shall be liable for a penalty of up to $500 for a
first offense, up to $750 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for each
subsequent offense, which shall be collected and enforced by summary
proceedings pursuant to the "Penalty Enforcement Law of 1999,"
P.L.1999, c.274 (C.2A:58-10 et seq.).  The Superior Court, Law Division,
Special Civil Part in the county in which the residential rental property is

Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs in the Department of Law and
Public Safety or the Attorney General.  Following the proceedings, the amount
wrongfully charged shall be taken from the collected penalty and shall be
remitted to the applicant or prospective tenant.
c.  The requirements of subsection a. of this section
shall not apply to:
(1) a dwelling unit
located in a one-family or two-family dwelling that is offered for rent; or
(2)  a licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate
Commission, unless the licensee is the landlord of the residential rental
property.

rules.title: Annual adjustment and publication of the application fee limit
rules.requirement: Beginning January 1, 2027, the Division of Consumer Affairs Director must adjust the application fee limit annually in direct proportion to a positive percentage change over the 12 months ending the preceding October 31 in the specified Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island Metropolitan Area, All Items (1982-84=100); no adjustment is made unless that change is greater than zero. The State Treasurer must determine the adjustment by December 1 for fees charged in the following calendar year beginning January 1, and the Director must publish the applicable limit annually on the division's website.
rules.key_value: Annual adjustment only for positive change in the specified CPI
rules.coverage_conditions: These administrative duties apply to the Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs in the Department of Law and Public Safety and the State Treasurer in administering the application or similar fee limit for applications to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes. The underlying limit applies to landlords and their agents, excludes dwelling units located in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent, and excludes New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees unless the licensee is the property's landlord. Annual adjustments begin January 1 of the year following enactment and apply only when the specified CPI percentage change is greater than zero.
rules.exemptions: The underlying fee limitation excludes units in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent and New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees who are not the property's landlord.

rules.title: Application fee regulations and violation reporting mechanism
rules.requirement: The Division of Consumer Affairs Director must adopt rules and regulations as necessary to implement the act in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act, including rules establishing a mechanism for applicants or prospective tenants to report violations. The Director must make that reporting mechanism available on the division's website.
rules.coverage_conditions: The duty applies to the Director of the Division of Consumer Affairs in the Department of Law and Public Safety when implementing P.L.2025, c.405, and the reporting mechanism serves applicants or prospective tenants reporting violations of that act. Its underlying application fee limit covers landlords and their agents requiring application or similar fees to apply to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes, except units located in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent and New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensees who are not the property's landlord.
rules.exemptions: The reporting mechanism concerns violations of this act; the underlying fee limit retains its one-family and two-family dwelling exemption and its exemption for real estate licensees who are not the property's landlord.

rules.title: Prohibition on discriminatory rental decisions
rules.requirement: Property owners and landlords must not discriminate in renting housing based on race, color, religion, disability, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, marital status, rental assistance, family status, or military status. Prohibited conduct includes refusing rental assistance, discriminatory neighborhood steering, refusing a family because the property has lead paint, and discriminatory rental terms or fees.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to property owners and landlords renting residential housing in Boston and their treatment of tenants and prospective tenants based on the listed protected characteristics. Rental assistance includes Section 8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers; family status includes having children. The source supplies no property-size or owner-occupancy exceptions.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory rent increases
rules.requirement: Any person or agent who threatens or takes a retaliatory rent increase against a residential tenant for protected activity is liable for the greater of actual damages or an award of one to three months' rent, plus suit costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. A qualifying rent-increase notice within six months creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and the same action at the same time regardless of protected activity or belief in it; any lease or rental-agreement waiver is void and unenforceable.
rules.key_value: Retaliatory increases prohibited; six-month rebuttable presumption
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person or agent thereof threatening or taking reprisals against a tenant of residential premises because the tenant: commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in a judicial or administrative action seeking damages under or enforcement of federal, state, or local law, regulation, by-law, or ordinance regulating residential premises; exercised rights under chapter 164, section 124D; reported a violation or suspected violation of a health or building code or other law, regulation, or municipal by-law or ordinance regulating residential premises to the board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; reported or complained of such a violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or landlord's agent; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization; or made or expressed an intention to make a rent payment to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A, section 6(c). For the rent-increase presumption, the tenant must receive notice of an increase within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such an action, exercised such rights, made such a report or complaint, or organized or joined such a tenants' union, or within six months after another person took such action or actions on the tenant's behalf or in, or relating to, the building where the tenant resides. The six-month period governs the presumption and does not establish a time limit on the underlying reprisal liability. The presumption requires clear and convincing rebuttal evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and that the action would have occurred in the same manner and at the same time regardless of tenants' protected activity or the belief that tenants engaged in it. Waivers in any lease or other rental agreement are void and unenforceable.
rules.quoted_span:
Section 18. Any person or agent thereof who threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises for the tenant's act of, commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in any judicial or administrative action the purpose of which action is to obtain damages under, or otherwise enforce, any federal, state or local law, regulation, by-law or ordinance, which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or exercising the tenant's rights pursuant to section one hundred and twenty-four D of chapter one hundred and sixty-four; or reporting to the board of health or, in the city of Boston to the commissioner of housing inspection or to any other board having as its objective the regulation of residential premises a violation or a suspected violation of any health or building code or of any other municipal by-law or ordinance, or state or federal law or regulation which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or to the agent of the landlord; or for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization, or for making or expressing an intention to make, a payment of rent to an organization of unit owners pursuant to paragraph (c) of section six of chapter one hundred and eighty-three A shall be liable for damages which shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, and the costs of the suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee.
The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.
Any waiver of this provision in any lease or other rental agreement shall be void and unenforceable.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory tenancy termination
rules.requirement: Any person or agent who threatens or takes retaliatory tenancy termination against a residential tenant for protected activity is liable for the greater of actual damages or an award of one to three months' rent, plus suit costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. A qualifying termination notice within six months, except for nonpayment of rent, creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and the same action at the same time regardless of protected activity or belief in it; any lease or rental-agreement waiver is void and unenforceable.
rules.key_value: Retaliatory termination prohibited; six-month rebuttable presumption
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person or agent thereof threatening or taking reprisals against a tenant of residential premises because the tenant: commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in a judicial or administrative action seeking damages under or enforcement of federal, state, or local law, regulation, by-law, or ordinance regulating residential premises; exercised rights under chapter 164, section 124D; reported a violation or suspected violation of a health or building code or other law, regulation, or municipal by-law or ordinance regulating residential premises to the board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; reported or complained of such a violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or landlord's agent; organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization; or made or expressed an intention to make a rent payment to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A, section 6(c). For the termination presumption, the tenant must receive a notice of termination, except for nonpayment of rent, within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such an action, exercised such rights, made such a report or complaint, or organized or joined such a tenants' union, or within six months after another person took such action or actions on the tenant's behalf or in, or relating to, the building where the tenant resides. The nonpayment exception applies to the termination-notice presumption, not to the underlying reprisal liability. The six-month period governs the presumption and does not establish a time limit on that liability. The presumption requires clear and convincing rebuttal evidence of no reprisal, sufficient independent justification, and that the action would have occurred in the same manner and at the same time regardless of tenants' protected activity or the belief that tenants engaged in it. Waivers in any lease or other rental agreement are void and unenforceable.
rules.exemptions: Termination notices for nonpayment of rent are excluded from the rebuttable presumption; the text does not make nonpayment a general exemption from reprisal liability.
rules.quoted_span:

Any person or agent thereof who threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises for the tenant's act of, commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in any judicial or administrative action the purpose of which action is to obtain damages under, or otherwise enforce, any federal, state or local law, regulation, by-law or ordinance, which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or exercising the tenant's rights pursuant to section one hundred and twenty-four D of chapter one hundred and sixty-four; or reporting to the board of health or, in the city of Boston to the commissioner of housing inspection or to any other board having as its objective the regulation of residential premises a violation or a suspected violation of any health or building code or of any other municipal by-law or ordinance, or state or federal law or regulation which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or to the agent of the landlord; or for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization, or for making or expressing an intention to make, a payment of rent to an organization of unit owners pursuant to paragraph (c) of section six of chapter one hundred and eighty-three A shall be liable for damages which shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, and the costs of the suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee.
The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. rules.title: Notice of tenants’ rights when ending occupancy
rules.requirement: Covered landlords and foreclosing owners must provide the Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources when starting eviction, declining lease renewal, or asking a tenant or former homeowner to leave, delivering it together with the applicable termination notice. This is a notification requirement and does not establish permissible grounds for eviction.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in Boston, including purchasers of property out of foreclosure or from a bank or mortgage lender asking former owners or tenants to leave. Excludes residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility, and residences in a nonprofit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug or other substance abuse.
rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; residences in a nonprofit facility whose primary purpose is providing short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug or other substance abuse.
rules.citation: Housing Stability Notification Act, Sec. 10-11.7; Tenant FAQs, questions 1, 4 and 5
rules.quoted_span:
The Housing Stability Notification Act (HSNA) is an Ordinance passed by the City of
Boston in October 2020 that requires any landlord planning to end a tenancy
agreement to provide the tenant with a Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources.
The HSNA requires that landlords give this Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources
to tenants when the landlord starts the eviction process, or when the landlord
decides to not offer the tenant a renewal of their lease agreement. The Notice of
Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to
Quit.
The Notice of Tenants’ Rights and Resources must also be delivered to any tenant
that is asked to leave a property. For example, if someone is purchasing a property
out of foreclosure, or from a bank or a mortgage lender, they must provide this
Notice to the former owners of the property, or any tenants that live in the
property.

rules.title: Criminal-history inquiries, checks and disclosure
rules.requirement: Subject to the listed exemptions, rental housing providers must not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection or decision-making, or require disclosure or authorization for release of criminal history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental housing providers in Berkeley dealing with current or prospective tenants. The source lists exemptions for lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties with 1–3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back to their home in accordance with BMC 13.76.130 A.9; and units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates. The source does not supply the specific requirements for each exemption, so their application requires execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
On April 14, 2020, Berkeley City Council passed the Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance (BMC 13.106). An overview of the ordinance is available below. Please review the Ordinance for more specific details related to your property or tenancy.
It is unlawful to do any of the following with regard to current or prospective tenants
Inquire about criminal history
Indicate that persons with criminal backgrounds will not be considered for housing, including in rental advertisements, application materials, or verbally
Refuse to rent or terminate a tenancy based on criminal history
Require disclosure or authorization for release of criminal history

rules.title: Individual consideration of criminal history
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers must not categorically deny housing to everyone with arrests or convictions and must consider applicants individually, subject to the policy's criminal-history exceptions.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; the policy also applies through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. The criminal-history guidance excludes current criminal behavior and situations involving a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety. It does not govern where federal or state law imposes a conflicting criminal-history requirement.
rules.exemptions: Current criminal behavior; a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety; conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, introductory provisions
rules.quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.

rules.title: Excluded criminal records in eligibility and eviction decisions
rules.requirement: Covered Developers/Agents must not consider arrests without convictions, convictions subject to judicial relief, juvenile records, or convictions more than five years old when determining housing eligibility or considering eviction. The policy excludes current criminal behavior and specified conviction-related safety or housing circumstances, and yields to conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements.
rules.key_value: Convictions more than 5 years old excluded, subject to exceptions
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Developers/Agents determining housing eligibility or considering eviction for housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; the policy also applies through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. Excluded records include dismissed charges, diversion programs and similar non-convictions; convictions subject to expungement, sealing, certificates for relief from disabilities or other judicial relief; juvenile records; and convictions more than five years old. The criminal-history guidance excludes current criminal behavior and situations involving a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety. It does not govern where federal or state law imposes a conflicting criminal-history requirement.
rules.exemptions: Current criminal behavior; a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety; conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, paragraph 1(a)–(d)
rules.quoted_span:
1. The Developer/Agent (Agent) agrees to not consider any of the following categories when 
determining housing eligibility and or considering eviction: 
 
a) Arrests that did not result in conviction. This includes dismissed charges, diversion 
programs, and similar non-convictions. 
b) Convictions that are subject to a form of judicial relief, such as expungement, sealing, 
and certificates for relief from disabilities. 
c) Juvenile records 
d) A conviction more than 5 years old. Tenant selection policy related to arrests and 
convictions does not apply in situations where there is: 
 
 A direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and or unreasonable 
risk of substantial harm to the safety of others.  
 Landlords would consider additional factors such as: evidence of rehabilitation, the time 
that has elapsed since the conviction occurred, and/or the age of the person at the time 
the conviction occurred. 
 This guidance does not apply to current criminal behavior.

rules.title: Credit scores excluded from housing decisions
rules.requirement: A covered Agent must not use an applicant's credit score to approve or deny a housing application.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Agent approving or denying a residential housing application for a housing provider receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy. The policy also applies to residential tenant selection through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, Credit paragraph 5(a)
rules.quoted_span:
a) The agent agrees not to use the applicant credit score to approve or deny housing    
applications.

rules.title: Credit history only substitutes for unavailable rental history
rules.requirement: Covered Property Managers may use an applicant's credit history only in place of unavailable rental history to determine the applicant's ability to pay rent.
rules.key_value: Only when rental history is unavailable
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Property Managers considering an applicant's credit history for a housing provider receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and to residential tenant selection under the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. Credit history may be used only to determine ability to pay rent, in lieu of rental history when rental history is unavailable.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, Credit paragraph 5(b)
rules.quoted_span:
b) Property Managers may consider an applicant’s credit history, but such information may 
ONLY be used in lieu of rental history to determine an applicant’s ability to pay rent when rental 
history is not available.

rules.title: Evidence of ability and willingness to pay rent
rules.requirement: An applicant's ability and willingness to pay rent must be demonstrated through an identifiable source of sufficient income and prior rental history. The policy permits credit history to substitute for rental history when rental history is unavailable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to applicants undergoing residential tenant selection by housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. The income and prior-rental-history demonstration is subject to the express permission for Property Managers to use credit history in lieu of rental history to determine ability to pay rent when rental history is unavailable.
rules.exemptions: Credit history may substitute for unavailable rental history for the specified ability-to-pay determination.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, Credit paragraphs 5(b)–(c)
rules.quoted_span:
b) Property Managers may consider an applicant’s credit history, but such information may 
ONLY be used in lieu of rental history to determine an applicant’s ability to pay rent when rental 
history is not available. Where insufficient credit is the basis for rejection, mitigating 
circumstances may include: 
 
 a representative payer or other reliable third party who would take written responsibility for 
payment; 
 evidence that insufficient credit was the result of a disability;  
 evidence that insufficient credit was the result of other circumstances and there is reason to 
believe that applicant will now pay rent promptly and in full. 
 
  c) An applicant’s ability and willingness to pay rent must be demonstrated through an 
identifiable source of sufficient income to pay rent and prior rental history.

rules.title: Lack of credit history insufficient for rejection
rules.requirement: A covered housing provider may not reject an applicant solely for lacking credit history; the policy distinguishes lack of credit history from poor credit history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential applicants evaluated by housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. This restriction concerns lack of credit history, as distinguished from poor credit history, as the justification for rejection.
rules.exemptions: The provision distinguishes poor credit history from lack of credit history.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, Credit paragraph 5(c)
rules.quoted_span:
The lack of credit 
history, as opposed to poor credit history, is not sufficient justification to reject an applicant.

rules.title: Consider demonstrated higher rent burden
rules.requirement: A covered Agent must take rent burden into account when an applicant demonstrates a history of satisfying a higher rent burden than the Agent normally uses.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Agents evaluating residential applicants for housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. rules.quoted_span:
An 
Agent must also take into account rent burden if an applicant can demonstrate a history of

rules.title: Care and prompt return of sensitive verification documents
rules.requirement: A covered Agent must handle sensitive or confidential mitigating-circumstance information with utmost care and promptly return all documents containing it after review. If the applicant refuses to provide or permit access to reasonably needed verification information, the Agent may stop considering that mitigating circumstance.
rules.key_value: Prompt return after review
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Agents handling sensitive or confidential information in verification of mitigating circumstances under the policy's credit provisions for housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy, and through the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. An Agent may request information reasonably needed for verification, including confidential information; refusal to provide or allow access to that further information permits the Agent to discontinue consideration of the mitigating circumstance.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy, Credit paragraph 5(d)
rules.quoted_span:
d) The Agent shall have the right to request information reasonably needed to verify the 
mitigating circumstances, even if such information is of a confidential nature (e.g. verifications 
from medical professionals that provide confidential information.). The Agent shall treat all 
sensitive or confidential information with utmost care and return any and all documents 
containing such information to the applicant promptly after review. If the applicant refuses to 
provide or give access to such further information the Agent may choose not to give further 
consideration to the mitigating circumstance.

rules.title: Proposed prohibition on lessors purchasing defined coordination services
rules.requirement: The bill would prohibit a real estate lessor, its agent or its subcontractor from subscribing to, contracting with or otherwise exchanging anything of value for a defined service provider’s services. For successful enforcement, the proposal would award plaintiffs court-determined action costs, reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and investigation costs, including awards to a successfully enforcing attorney general or municipality; on a plaintiff’s prompt motion, the court could award simple interest on actual damages from service of the pleading asserting the chapter claim through judgment, or a shorter period within that interval.
rules.exemptions: A residential dwelling unit is a house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended as a person’s primary residence, excluding inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities. A real estate lessor is an individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust or unincorporated organization that owns real property and leases all or part of it as a residential dwelling unit. A service provider is a person performing a coordination function for any real estate lessor or rentor; person includes a natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm or association. Coordination comprises collecting the specified historical or contemporaneous actual rent, price-change, supply, occupancy or lease-termination and renewal information, analyzing or processing that information, and recommending rental prices, lease terms, occupancy levels or another commercial term to a real estate lessor. Publication of a fair market rent calculated using publicly available data is excluded from a recommendation. Computation is included but is not required by the definition. These are qualifications of the regulated actors and services, not findings about actual activity at an address.
rules.citation: H.5222, 194th General Court, proposed G.L. c. 40Z, §§ 1, 2(a), 3(b), 3(d)
rules.quoted_span:
“Coordinate”, with respect to a service provider, the:
(i) collecting of historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units;
(ii) analyzing or processing of the information described in clause (i), including with the use of a system, software or process that uses computation; and
(iii) recommending of rental prices, lease terms, occupancy levels, or other commercial term to a real estate lessor, provided that publication of a fair market rent calculated using publicly available data shall not constitute a recommendation.
“Person”, any natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm or association.
“Predispute arbitration agreement”, an agreement to arbitrate a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.
“Predispute joint-action waiver”, an agreement, whether or not part of a predispute arbitration agreement, that would prohibit or waive the right of one of the parties to participate in a joint, class or collective action in a judicial, arbitral, administrative or other forum, concerning a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.
“Real estate lessor”, any individual, corporation, partnership, association, joint-stock company, trust or unincorporated organization that owns real property and leases such property or any portion thereof in the form of a residential dwelling unit.
“Residential dwelling unit”, any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended to be used as a person’s primary residence; provided, that “residential dwelling unit” shall not include inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities.
“Service provider”, any person that performs a coordination function for any real estate lessor or rentor.
Section 2. (a) No real estate lessor, or any agent or subcontractor thereof, shall subscribe to, contract with or otherwise exchange anything of value in return for the services of a service provider.
(b) No service provider shall facilitate an agreement to not compete among real estate lessors with respect to residential dwelling units.
Section 3. (a) A violation of this section shall also constitute an unfair method of competition, and a violation of the provisions of chapter 93 and chapter 93A. Nothing in this section shall impair or limit the applicability of either chapter or the antitrust laws, generally.
(b) Pursuant to a motion by the plaintiff promptly made, the court may award simple interest on actual damages sustained by the plaintiff for the period beginning on the date of service of the pleading of the plaintiff setting forth a claim under this chapter and ending on the date of judgment, or for any shorter period therein.
(c) At the election of the person alleging conduct constituting a violation of this section, or the named representative of a class or in a collective action alleging such conduct, no predispute arbitration agreement or predispute joint-action waiver shall be valid or enforceable with respect to a case which is filed under federal, tribal or state or local law and relates to a violation of this chapter.
(d) In the case of any successful action to enforce liability pursuant to this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation as determined by the court shall be awarded to plaintiffs. Costs and attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation shall be awarded to the attorney general or municipality where the attorney general or municipality successfully enforces this chapter.

rules.title: Proposed prohibition on algorithmic rent setting and occupancy determinations
rules.requirement: The pending bill would prohibit lessors and landlords from employing, using or relying on a defined algorithmic device or coordinator to set or change rent or determine occupancy levels for residential dwelling units, subject to the definitions and product exclusions below. A violation would violate Chapter 93A, section 2 and carry a civil penalty of no more than $5,000 per violation, with each rent determination, increase or setting under subsection (b) counted separately; successful enforcement plaintiffs, including the attorney general or a municipality when successfully enforcing the chapter, would receive action costs, reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and investigation costs as determined by the court.
rules.key_value: Proposed prohibition; civil penalty up to $5,000 per violation
rules.exemptions: Address scope is a house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended for use as a primary residence in Massachusetts. An algorithmic device is a computational process derived from machine learning or other artificial intelligence techniques that processes or calculates nonpublic competitor data to advise a lessor or landlord about rent; it excludes trade-association reports published periodically but no more frequently than monthly that receive renter data and publish it in an aggregated and anonymous matter, and products used to establish rent or income limits under affordable-housing program guidelines of a local government, the commonwealth, the federal government or another political subdivision. These are product exclusions, not blanket exemptions for affordable-housing properties. A coordinator is any person operating an algorithmic device, software or data analytics service that performs a coordinating function for a residential rental property lessor or landlord, including a lessor or landlord performing that function for their own benefit. A coordinating function uses nonpublic competitor data and includes collecting specified rent, supply or termination and renewal data from two or more lessors or landlords; computationally analyzing or processing those data, including algorithm training; and recommending rental prices, lease renewal terms or ideal occupancy levels. Nonpublic competitor data must be information not widely available or easily accessible to the public, derived from or otherwise provided by another lessor or landlord, whether attributable to a particular competitor or anonymized. Person includes natural persons, corporations, partnerships, companies, trusts and associations of persons. The proposal does not prohibit all pricing tools, and this extraction does not establish that any actor or product meets these definitions.
rules.citation: Massachusetts S.2983, 194th General Court, proposed G.L. c. 186, § 15G(a)–(d)
rules.quoted_span:
Section 15G. (a) As used in this section, the following words shall have the following meanings unless the context clearly requires otherwise:
"Algorithmic device", any computational process derived from machine learning or other artificial intelligence techniques, that processes or calculates nonpublic competitor data for the purpose of advising a lessor or landlord concerning the amount of rent that the lessor or landlord may consider charging a tenant; provided, however that "algorithmic device" shall not include: (i) any report published periodically, but not more frequently than monthly, by a trade association that receives renter data and publishes it in an aggregated and anonymous matter; or (ii) a product used for the purpose of establishing rent or income limits in accordance with the affordable housing program guidelines of a local government, the commonwealth, the federal government or other political subdivision.
“Coordinating function”, any action utilizing nonpublic competitor data that includes: (i) collecting historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, supply levels or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units from two or more rental property lessors or landlords; (ii) analyzing or processing of historical or contemporaneous actual rent prices, supply levels or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates of residential dwelling units from two or more rental property lessors or landlords through use of a system, software or process that uses computation, including by using the information to train an algorithm; and (iii) recommending rental prices, lease renewal terms or ideal occupancy levels to a rental property lessor or landlord.
"Coordinator", any person who operates an algorithmic device, software or data analytics service that performs a coordinating function for any residential rental property lessor or landlord, including a residential rental property lessor or landlord performing a coordinating function for their own benefit.
"Nonpublic competitor data", information that is not widely available or easily accessible to the public, including information about actual rent prices, occupancy rates, lease start and end dates, and similar data, regardless of whether the data are attributable to a specific competitor or anonymized, and that is derived from or otherwise provided by any other lessor or landlord.
“Person”, any natural person or persons, or any corporation, partnership, company, trust or association of persons.
"Residential Dwelling Unit", any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended to be used as a primary residence in the state.
(b) In setting the amount of rent to be charged to a tenant for the occupancy of a residential dwelling unit, determining any change in the amount of rent to be charged to a tenant for the renewed occupancy of a residential dwelling unit, or otherwise determining what amount to charge a tenant to rent a residential dwelling unit, or determining occupancy levels of residential dwelling units, no lessor or landlord shall employ, use or rely upon an algorithmic device or coordinator.
(c) A violation of this section shall constitute a violation of section 2 of Chapter 93A. The civil penalty for each violation of this section shall not exceed $5,000 per violation. For the purposes of this section, each time a rent is determined, increased or otherwise set under subsection (b) shall constitute a single and separate violation.
(d) In the case of any successful action to enforce liability pursuant to this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation as determined by the court shall be awarded to plaintiffs. Costs and attorney fees, expert fees and the costs of investigation shall be awarded to the attorney general or municipality where the attorney general or municipality successfully enforces this chapter.

rules.title: Prohibition on obtaining defined coordinator services
rules.requirement: A rental property owner, or its agent, representative, or subcontractor, may not receive, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange consideration for the use of a defined coordinator’s services. This conduct is unlawful and violates the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: A coordinator is a person operating algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function for a rental property owner, including an owner acting for its own benefit. An algorithmic device excludes a spreadsheet operating without artificial intelligence and requiring human analysis to process or calculate data, and a database whose only algorithmic use is querying stored unprocessed data. A coordinating function encompasses collecting two or more owners’ competitively sensitive information for algorithmic or automated analysis used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy levels; setting those terms through an algorithm or automated process analyzing another owner’s competitively sensitive information; or setting or recommending those terms for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Information used to train an algorithm is included. Competitively sensitive information is nonpublic information, and information combined with public information remains nonpublic; nonpublic means unavailable to the public at no cost. Excluded functions are research, statistical analysis, or testing without use in setting or recommending current or future lease terms; publicly available, free rent estimates; qualifying real estate brokerage databases available equally to subscribers that neither set or recommend the specified terms nor collect competitively sensitive information for doing so; and lawful government affordability controls. Government entities lawfully imposing affordability controls are also excluded from coordinator status. Parallel pricing coordination requires a tacit or express agreement concerning pricing of reasonably interchangeable residential units, including coordinator agreements with multiple owners, and excludes pricing actions required by affordability controls. Affordability controls are rent restrictions under government programs, including the listed housing programs and rent control or rent leveling ordinances; this is a conduct qualification, not a blanket exemption for affordable properties. A controlling-interest holder and the entity owning a rental residential unit count as one rental property owner. The address must be intended as a primary residence and cannot be inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, or a detention or correctional facility.

rules.title: Coordinator prohibition on facilitating anticompetitive agreements
rules.requirement: A defined coordinator may not facilitate a tacit or express agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition concerning residential dwelling units, including by performing a defined coordinating function. This conduct is unlawful and violates the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: This duty applies to the coordinator, including an owner acting as a coordinator for its own benefit. A coordinator operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device performing a coordinating function; lawful government affordability-control activity is excluded. Algorithmic devices exclude non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis to process or calculate data, and databases using an algorithm only to query stored unprocessed data. Coordinating functions encompass collection of two or more owners’ competitively sensitive information for algorithmic or automated processing used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy levels; setting those terms through algorithmic or automated processing of another owner’s competitively sensitive information; and setting or recommending those terms for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Algorithm training is included where specified. Competitively sensitive information is nonpublic; information unavailable publicly at no cost, including combinations with public information, remains nonpublic. Exclusions cover research, statistical analysis, or testing without use to set or recommend current or future lease terms; rent estimates made publicly available free of charge; equally available subscriber real estate brokerage databases that neither set or recommend the specified terms nor collect competitively sensitive information for doing so; and lawful government affordability controls. Parallel pricing coordination concerns tacit or express agreements to raise, change, maintain, or manipulate prices for reasonably interchangeable residential units, including coordinator agreements with multiple owners, unless required by affordability controls. Those controls are government-program rent restrictions, including rent control and rent leveling ordinances; affordable-property status alone is not an exemption. A controlling-interest holder and the unit-owning entity count as one owner. Tacit agreement means mutual consent without verbal or written communication, potentially demonstrated by a pattern of conduct. Units must be intended as primary residences and exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.

rules.title: Prohibition on engaging in or facilitating parallel pricing coordination
rules.requirement: Two or more persons may not engage in or otherwise facilitate defined parallel pricing coordination: tacit or express agreements between two or more rental property owners, including agreements between a coordinator and multiple owners, to raise, change, maintain, or manipulate leasing prices for reasonably interchangeable residential dwelling units, unless required by affordability controls. This conduct is unlawful and violates the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: A rental property owner owns one or more rental residential dwelling units directly or indirectly; a controlling-interest holder and the entity owning a unit are treated as a single owner. Tacit agreement means mutual consent without verbal or written communication, which may but need not be demonstrated by a pattern of conduct. The exception concerns pricing actions required by affordability controls, meaning rent restrictions established under government programs, including rent control or rent leveling ordinances; it does not categorically exempt affordable properties. Persons include natural persons, corporations, partnerships, companies, trusts, and associations unless context requires otherwise. A coordinator operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device performing a defined coordinating function, including an owner acting for its own benefit, subject to the statutory device and coordinating-function exclusions. This prohibition requires the defined agreement; it does not establish that any particular pricing tool or conduct meets that definition. Address scope excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities and requires intended primary-residence use.

rules.title: Prohibition on performing a defined coordinating function
rules.requirement: Any person is prohibited from performing a coordinating function as defined by the Act, subject to its research, free public rent estimate, qualifying brokerage database, and lawful government affordability-control exclusions. Performing such a function is unlawful and violates the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: A coordinating function is: collecting competitively sensitive information of two or more rental property owners for algorithmic or automated analysis or processing, including training, where that process is used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy levels; setting those terms through an algorithm or automated process analyzing or processing another owner’s competitively sensitive information, including training; or setting or recommending those terms for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Competitively sensitive information is nonpublic information, including prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, termination and renewal dates, and other material lease terms. Information unavailable to the public at no cost is nonpublic, and combinations with public information are treated as nonpublic. Exclusions apply to providing, using, or collecting that information solely for research, statistical analysis, or testing when it is not used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, fees, occupancy rates or levels, or other current or future lease terms; developing rent estimates made publicly available at no cost; using equally available subscriber brokerage databases listing properties for rent or sale that neither set or recommend the specified terms nor collect competitively sensitive information for doing so; and lawful government affordability controls. Parallel pricing coordination requires a tacit or express agreement between two or more owners concerning pricing of reasonably interchangeable units, including coordinator agreements with multiple owners, unless required by affordability controls. A controlling-interest holder and its unit-owning entity count as one owner. Affordability controls are government-program rent restrictions, including rent control and rent leveling ordinances; affordable-property status alone does not exempt an address. The prohibition applies to any person and does not require coordinator status. rules.title: Prohibition on using defined rent-coordination service providers
rules.requirement: A real estate lessor—an owner leasing real property or a portion of it as a residential dwelling unit—or its agent or subcontractor may not subscribe to, contract with, exchange anything of value for, or otherwise use the services of a service provider as defined in the ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Residential dwelling units must be intended as a person's primary residence and exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. A service provider is a person performing a coordination function, with the source's express cross-reference to Section 1(a)(i)(1), for a real estate lessor or rentor. Person includes a natural person, corporation, partnership, limited liability company, firm, or association. The coordination definition describes collecting nonpublic competitor information from real estate lessors; collecting historical or contemporaneous prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease or rental contract termination and renewal dates from two or more real estate lessors or public databases; computational analysis or processing of that information; and recommendations using that information concerning rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Nonpublic competitor information includes prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates, or other material lease terms that are less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost. The coordination definition exempts owners of multiple properties for actions related exclusively to properties controlled by the same rental property owner. Licensed Real Estate Agents operating in accordance with all applicable state regulations are excluded from both the coordination and service-provider definitions. These are qualifications of the regulated actors and services, not findings that any address uses such a service.

rules.title: Prohibition on algorithmic rent fixing
rules.requirement: Landlords renting covered residential dwelling units in Hoboken must not use software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing real estate lessors. The Division of Housing or any private citizen alleging to be aggrieved may bring alleged violations to Hoboken Municipal Court; upon conviction, any person violating the chapter is subject to one or more penalties prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine not exceeding $2,000, or community service not exceeding 90 days.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers residential dwelling units in Hoboken used as primary residences, excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities. The source does not limit its medical exclusion to inpatient care or its long-term-care exclusion to licensed facilities; the available fact vocabulary cannot completely represent these exclusions.
rules.exemptions: Medical/long-term care and detention facilities are excluded from covered residential dwelling units. The prohibition concerns the defined collection and analysis of nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors for coordination, recommendation, or implementation among competing lessors, not all pricing tools. Nonpublic competitor information must be less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost; it includes, without limitation, prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates of residential dwelling units, and other material terms.
rules.quoted_span:
A.
Prohibited conduct. Landlords who rent any residential dwelling unit (defined as any primary residence excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities) in the City of Hoboken are prohibited from price fixing using algorithmic pricing.
For purposes of this chapter, "price fixing using algorithmic pricing" shall be defined as the use of software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units among competing real estate lessors.
For purposes of this chapter, "nonpublic competitor information" shall be defined as information including, but not limited to, prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease contract termination, renewal dates of residential dwelling units or any other material terms that is less than 365 days old and is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.
B.
Enforcement.
Enforcement. Alleged violations of this chapter may be brought by the Division of Housing, or any private citizen alleging to be aggrieved, to the Hoboken Municipal Court for adjudication.
C.
Penalties. Any person violating the requirements set forth in this chapter shall, upon conviction, be subject to one or more of the following penalties:
Penalties as prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5; or
By a fine not exceeding $2,000; or
By a period of community service not exceeding 90 days.

             4)     If the Landlord is reimbursed for Capital Improvements (i.e. –
                    insurance, court-awarded damages, subsidies, etc.), such
                    reimbursement must be deducted from the Capital Improvements
                    before costs are amortized and allocated among the Rental Units.

rules.title: Tenant petitions and filing deadlines
rules.requirement: A covered tenant may petition to review an excessive increase, reduce rent for decreased services or uninhabitability, contest an unauthorized or excessive capital-improvement pass-through, or address another Article violation. Applicable filing limits are 30 days after service of an increase notice, 30 days after learning of noncompliance when required notice was omitted, and 180 days after other alleged violations.
rules.key_value: 30-day rent-review deadlines; 180 days for other violations
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Tenant entitled to occupy a nonexempt Santa Ana Rental Unit and responsible for or agreeing to pay its rent, filing with the Program Administrator under Division 3. Rent-regulation exemptions include certificates issued after February 1, 1995 and other applicable Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome agreements longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to another, and other applicable Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K–12 schools; housing issued a certificate within the previous 15 years; continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception with neither unit an ADU or junior ADU; and separately alienable dwellings whose owner is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and whose tenants receive the prescribed notice, included in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Petitions proceed under section 8-3145 and applicable regulations; no petition proceeds when a decision on the same or substantially the same grounds was made within the previous 180 days. Applicable standards include reasonable notice to the landlord and an opportunity to correct the conditions. The specified July 1, 2023 commencement subject to Council modification, annual exemption-claim provisions and incorporated statutory exemptions require execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
(a)   Effective July 1, 2023, or as modified by resolution of the City Council, a
Tenant may submit a Petition to the Program Administrator in accordance with the
procedures set forth in this Division on any one (1) or more of the following grounds:

              1)     To request review of a Rent Increase in excess of the maximum
                     allowed Rent Increase;
              2)     To request a reduction in Rent based on decreased Housing
                     Services;
              3)     To request a reduction in Rent based on failure of the Landlord to
                     maintain a habitable premises, including health, safety, fire, or
                     building code violations;
              4)     To contest a Capital Improvement cost as an unauthorized or
                     excessive pass through; or,
              5)     For any other violation of this Article by the Landlord.


       (b)    Tenant’s time to file a Petition. Where applicable, a Tenant filing a Petition
under this Division shall do so within the following time limits:

              2)     In instances where notice is not provided as required, the Tenant

                     Tenant knew of the alleged failure to comply with the requirements
                     of this Article; and,
              3)     For any other violation(s) of this Article by the Landlord, the Tenant
                     shall file a Petition within one hundred and eighty (180) days of the
                     alleged violation(s).

rules.title: Noncompliance bars landlord petitions and upward adjustments
rules.requirement: No landlord petition or upward rent adjustment under Division 3 is authorized if the landlord continues noncompliance after a Board order or has failed to bring the unit into compliance with the implied warranty of habitability.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord seeking a petition or upward adjustment under Santa Ana Division 3 for a Rental Unit subject to that Division, where either stated noncompliance condition exists. Landlord includes owners, lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives with authority to bind the landlord. Rent-regulation exemptions encompass post-February 1, 1995 certificates and other Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome leases longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to others, and other Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; certificates issued within the previous 15 years; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception without ADUs or junior ADUs; and separately alienable housing with an owner that is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and the prescribed tenant notice, in the agreement for post-effective-date commencements or renewals. Annual exemption claims and incorporated statutory exemptions require execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
No Landlord Petition or upward adjustment of Rent shall be authorized
under this Division if the Landlord:

              1)     Has continued to fail to comply, after order of the Board, with any
                     provisions of this Article and/or orders or regulations issued
                     thereunder by the Board; or,
              2)     Has failed to bring the Rental Unit into compliance with the implied
                     warranty of habitability.

rules.title: Compliance and registration prerequisites for increases
rules.requirement: A rent increase is ineffective if the owner fails substantial Division 3 compliance, applicable maintenance requirements, or City- or court-ordered repairs. No increase takes effect without accurately completed unit registration.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner/Landlord, including lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord, increasing rent for Santa Ana residential real property or mobilehome spaces subject to Division 3. Excludes certificates issued after February 1, 1995 and other Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome agreements longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to others, and other Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; certificates issued within the previous 15 years; continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception with neither unit an ADU or junior ADU; and separately alienable dwellings with a non-REIT, noncorporate owner and no corporate LLC member, plus the prescribed exemption notice, in the agreement for commencements or renewals after effectiveness. The section 8-3148(b) maintenance test expressly excepts mobilehomes and spaces subject, as applicable, to the Mobilehome Parks Act, Manufactured Housing Act or federal National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act. Incorporated statutory exemptions, maintenance regimes and annual exemption claims require execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
No Rent Increase shall be effective if the Owner:

       (a)     Fails to substantially comply with all provisions of this Division, including
but not limited to the failure to provide notices as required; or
