rules.title: Rent-stabilization notices and City filing
rules.requirement: Owners must provide the prescribed commencement notice and include Division 3 and petition-response information in increase notices, subject to the approved-fair-return exception, in English and the tenancy-negotiation language. Required landlord-to-tenant notices and documents must also go to the City through the Rental Registry, and no increase takes effect until Division 3 requirements are met.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner of Santa Ana residential real property or a mobilehome space subject to section 8-3149; Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord. Commencement notices are due on or before tenancy commencement; increase notices must disclose petition-response rights unless the increase follows an approved Fair Return Petition. Rent-regulation exemptions include post-February 1, 1995 certificates and other Costa-Hawkins exemptions; qualifying mobilehome leases longer than one year, new spaces first offered on or after January 1, 1990, non-primary-residence mobilehomes not leased to others, and other Mobilehome Residency Law exemptions; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; certificates issued within the previous 15 years; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures from tenancy inception with neither unit an ADU or junior ADU; and separately alienable units with a non-REIT, noncorporate owner and no corporate LLC member, plus the prescribed exemption notice included in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Section 8-3149(d) also reaches notices or documents required by other federal, state or local law. Statutory exemptions, annual exemption claims and the reach of this broader filing provision require execution review.

rules.title: Rental Registry Fee pass-through limit
rules.requirement: After timely payment, a landlord may pass through at most 50% of the Registry Fee in twelve equal monthly installments, excluding it from rent-increase calculations; delinquent fees and penalties cannot be passed through. No portion may be charged to the specified affordable or subsidized tenants, and excess pass-through payments must be reimbursed.
rules.key_value: 50% of timely paid fee over 12 months; no pass-through for specified subsidized tenants
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord assessed a Rental Registry Fee for a Santa Ana Rental Unit subject to Article XIX, including owners, lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord, when passing that fee to tenants of the applicable unit. Permission requires timely payment; delinquency eliminates pass-through permission for both fee and penalties. No portion may be passed to tenants in housing restricted by deed, a government-agreement regulatory restriction or another recorded document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income households under Health and Safety Code section 50093, or housing subject to an agreement providing subsidies for such households under that section or comparable federal statutes. Article coverage and annual exemption claims require review: rent exemptions under section 8-3147 and termination exemptions under section 8-3120(e) are provision-specific and cannot be assumed to eliminate all Registry obligations.

rules.title: Registration prerequisite to advertising and collecting rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not advertise a covered unit for rent or demand or accept its rent without complete and accurate registration. Petitions, applications, claims, requests and rent increases cannot take effect without accurately completed registration.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord with a Santa Ana Rental Unit subject to Article XIX and its Rental Registry requirements, including owners, lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord. Complete registration requires all City fees and penalties to be paid and a complete, accurate form containing the information required by Division 4 and implementing policies. Registration duties include initial and annual registration, changes of ownership or management, re-registration after vacancy and re-rental, and registration after loss of exemption; annual exemption declarations and supporting documents are required under section 8-3160(d). Rent and termination exemptions are provision-specific, so neither alone establishes exemption from the entire Article or Registry. The stated October 1, 2023 enforcement commencement and the Article's later voter-approval effectiveness require review.

petition, application, claim or request, and no Rent increases shall take effect for any

rules.title: Just cause after thirty days of lawful occupancy
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied covered residential real property for 30 days, the owner may terminate only for just cause stated in a written termination notice.
rules.key_value: 30 days of continuous lawful occupancy
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner offering Santa Ana residential real property for rent, including lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord, after the tenant's continuous lawful occupancy for 30 days. Termination provisions exclude mobilehomes and mobilehome spaces subject to Civil Code section 798.56. Section 8-3120(e) excludes transient/tourist hotel occupancy; accommodations in nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended-care facilities, licensed elderly residential-care facilities or specified adult residential facilities; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K–12 schools; shared kitchen/bath housing where the owner maintains a principal residence; owner-occupied single-family residences, including those renting no more than two units or bedrooms, including ADUs or junior ADUs; duplexes continuously occupied by the owner as a principal residence since tenancy inception; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years; and specified deed-restricted or government-agreement affordable/subsidized housing for very-low-, low- or moderate-income households. Separately alienable dwellings are exempt only when the owner is neither a REIT, corporation nor LLC with a corporate member and tenants receive the prescribed notice, included in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed after ordinance effectiveness, with agreement placement optional for earlier tenancies. Just cause is governed by the specified at-fault and no-fault grounds and their qualifications in section 8-3120(b). Annual exemption-claim requirements and incorporated statutory definitions require execution review.

              Mobilehome Spaces in Mobilehome Parks subject to the termination

The Mobilehome Residency Law exclusion is phrased as concerning termination provisions; its relationship to the express mobilehome-space notice duty and annual exemption claims requires review.

rules.title: Criminal-activity grounds and restoration rights
rules.requirement: The criminal-activity eviction ground requires reporting to law enforcement within a reasonable time and applies only to the tenant who committed the specified activity. If that tenant is acquitted, found not guilty, or not charged within the limitations period, the owner must offer restoration of the tenancy if the same property is available.

Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and authorized representatives. Incorporated definitions and annual exemption claims require execution review.

rules.title: Protection for qualifying replacement subleases
rules.requirement: An owner cannot terminate for a qualifying one-for-one replacement sublease when the tenant requests permission in writing, remains in the property as a primary residence and receives no written response within a reasonable time. rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner and a tenant protected by section 8-3120 after 30 days of continuous lawful occupancy in Santa Ana, where the written sublease request replaces departed lease tenants one-for-one and the original tenant remains in the property as a primary residence. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord. rules.title: Owner-occupancy and rental-withdrawal qualifications

rules.title: Demolition or substantial-remodel return protections
rules.requirement: For the demolition-or-substantial-remodel ground, the owner must give advance notice of reoccupancy after repairs or, at the tenant's request, first refusal of an owner-held comparable vacant unit offered at comparable rent. If the owner seeks to rent the remodeled unit within six months after work is completed, the evicted tenant has first refusal to return unless the owner provides the tenant's written waiver.
rules.key_value: Six-month post-remodel right of first refusal
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner invoking section 8-3120(b)(2)(D) after a Santa Ana tenant's 30 days of continuous lawful occupancy. Substantial remodeling means permitted replacement or substantial modification of structural, electrical, plumbing or mechanical systems, or lawful hazardous-material abatement, that cannot reasonably occur safely with the tenant in place and requires at least 30 days' vacancy; cosmetic improvements or safely performable occupied work do not qualify. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and authorized representatives. Excludes Civil Code section 798.56 mobilehome terminations; transient/tourist hotels; specified nonprofit hospital, religious, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care and adult residential facilities; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; owner-principal-residence shared kitchen/bath housing; owner-occupied single-family residences including up to two rented units/bedrooms; duplexes continuously owner-occupied principally since tenancy inception; certificates issued within 15 years; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; and separately alienable dwellings with a non-REIT, noncorporate owner and no corporate LLC member plus prescribed notice, in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Relocation and notice duties also apply. Statutory definitions, annual exemption claims and the relationship of the express reoccupancy waiver to section 8-3120(j) require review.

rules.title: Opportunity to cure and notice contents
rules.requirement: Before terminating for a curable lease violation, the owner must give notice and an opportunity to cure; an uncured violation may then support a three-day notice to quit without another cure opportunity. A cease-or-correct notice must be dated, properly served, warn of possible eviction, identify the reasonable-accommodation right and Program Administrator contact number, and give specific supporting facts.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner pursuing just-cause termination for a curable lease violation after a Santa Ana tenant's 30 days of continuous lawful occupancy; service and cure requirements incorporate Code of Civil Procedure sections 1161(3) and 1162. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and authorized representatives. Excludes Civil Code section 798.56 mobilehome terminations; transient/tourist hotels; specified nonprofit hospital, religious, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care and adult residential facilities; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; shared kitchen/bath housing with an owner principally residing there; owner-occupied single-family residences including up to two rented units/bedrooms; duplexes continuously owner-occupied principally from tenancy inception; certificates issued within 15 years; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; and separately alienable dwellings with a non-REIT, noncorporate owner and no corporate LLC member plus prescribed notice, included in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Incorporated procedural statutes and annual exemption claims require review.

rules.title: No-fault relocation payment or rent waiver
rules.requirement: For a covered no-fault termination, regardless of income, the owner must notify the tenant of applicable rights and either pay three months of rent within 15 calendar days after notice service or waive the final three months in writing before rent is due, using the rent in effect when notice was issued and stating the waiver amount and that no final-three-month rent is due. Assistance is credited against other legally required relocation assistance, may be recovered as damages in a possession action if the tenant fails to vacate after notice expires, and failure to comply strictly renders the termination notice void.
rules.key_value: Three months' rent; payment within 15 calendar days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner issuing a no-fault notice under section 8-3120(b)(2) for a tenancy requiring just cause after 30 days of continuous lawful Santa Ana occupancy. Assistance is unavailable where a government agency or court determines that the tenant caused the conditions triggering the applicable governmental or court order or legal need to vacate. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and authorized representatives. Excludes Civil Code section 798.56 mobilehome terminations; transient/tourist hotels; specified nonprofit hospital, religious, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care and adult residential facilities; school-owned-and-operated dormitories; owner-principal-residence shared kitchen/bath housing; owner-occupied single-family residences including up to two rented units/bedrooms; duplexes continuously owner-occupied principally from tenancy inception; certificates issued within 15 years; specified restricted/subsidized affordable housing; and separately alienable dwellings with a non-REIT, noncorporate owner and no corporate LLC member plus prescribed notice, in agreements commenced or renewed after effectiveness. Incorporated definitions and annual exemption claims require review.

rules.title: Prescribed lease or written just-cause disclosure
rules.requirement: Owners must provide the prescribed just-cause statement in at least 12-point type through the specified lease addendum or written notice. For tenancies commenced or renewed after effectiveness, a separate notice must be signed by the tenant and copied to the tenant; for preexisting tenancies, written notice is due within 30 days after effectiveness or may be provided as a lease addendum.

rules.title: Mobilehome park sale notice and relocation planning
rules.requirement: At least 60 days before selling a mobilehome park, the owner must notify residents and prepare an impact report with a replacement and relocation plan adequately mitigating displaced residents' ability to find adequate mobilehome-park housing, as applicable.

The duty expressly concerns park residents and displacement impacts from the proposed sale, rather than a general sale of residential property. Section 8-3120(a)'s Mobilehome Residency Law exclusion concerns termination provisions, while subsection (i) expressly imposes this sale obligation; section 8-3120(e)'s residential exemptions, applicable Mobilehome Residency Law provisions and annual exemption claims require review to determine their application to a particular park.

rules.title: Termination notice, rent acceptance and City submission
rules.requirement: For an at-fault or no-fault termination, the owner must serve the required written notice identifying a qualifying cause in English and the tenancy-negotiation language, and must not accept consideration for occupancy beyond the terminated term as specified. Within five days after service, the owner must submit an accurate notice copy and proof of tenant service signed under penalty of perjury through the City Registry, and retain proof of City service.

Section 8-3121 incorporates Civil Code sections 1945–1946.5 and qualifying grounds under section 8-3120(b); the section-specific wording of exemptions and annual exemption claims requires execution review.

rules.title: Retaliatory termination and nonrenewal prohibited
rules.requirement: If retaliation is the owner's main intent and the tenant is not in rent default, the owner may not terminate, refuse renewal or cause involuntary departure; retaliation for exercising Article rights is also prohibited. Tenants may assert retaliation affirmatively or defensively regardless of elapsed time, but retaliation claims must be brought in court rather than administratively.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner, including a lessor, sublessor, successor or representative authorized to bind the landlord, acting against a Tenant in a Santa Ana tenancy under section 8-3122(a). The no-rent-default and main-retaliatory-intent conditions expressly qualify subsection (a)(1); subsection (a)(3) separately prohibits retaliation for exercising Article rights. Tenant and Tenancy use the Article's Rental Unit definition, which excludes units exempt under applicable Article provisions. Section 8-3120(e) exemptions are expressly limited to that section, so neither those exemptions nor the 30-day just-cause threshold is treated as an established exemption from section 8-3122; provision-specific Article coverage and annual exemption claims require execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
1) If the main intent of the Owner in terminating a Tenancy or refusing to
                renew a Tenancy is retaliatory in nature, and if the Tenant is not in
                default as to the payment of Rent, then the Owner may not terminate
                the Tenancy or refuse to renew the Tenancy or cause the Tenant to
                quit involuntarily.

             2) A Tenant may assert retaliation affirmatively or as a defense to the
                Owner’s action regardless of the period of time which has elapsed
                between the Tenant's assertion or exercise of rights under this Article
                and the alleged act of retaliation.

             3) Retaliation against a Tenant because of the Tenant's exercise of rights
                under this Article is prohibited. Retaliation claims may only be brought
                in court and may not be addressed administratively. A court may
                consider the protections afforded by this Article in evaluating a claim of
                retaliation.

rules.title: Harassment through services, repairs and rent handling
rules.requirement: Covered actors may not interrupt, withhold or threaten required housing services except for the stated outside-control or properly noticed interruptions. They may not in bad faith neglect required repairs, delay or mishandle repairs, renovate to harass, reject lawful rent payments, leave acceptable payments unprocessed over 30 days, or fail to maintain a rent-delivery address.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies under section 8-3122(b) to an Owner or person acting as principal or agent offering Santa Ana Residential Real Property for rent, or an owner's contractor, subcontractor or employee, with respect to property under any rental agreement, other tenancy or estate at will however created. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and representatives authorized to bind the landlord; Residential Real Property includes rooms, rental units, mobilehomes and spaces offered for rent. Service interruptions caused by events or actions outside the owner's control, and interruptions properly noticed as required by a signed rental agreement, are excluded from subsection (b)(1). Bad faith is required for subsection (b)(2)'s repair and payment acts. Section 8-3120(e)'s exemptions and 30-day threshold are not stated as exemptions from this separate section; provision-specific Rental Unit definitions and annual exemption claims require review where relevant.

rules.title: Abusive entry, coerced departure and threats prohibited
rules.requirement: Covered actors may not abuse access rights, including unjustified or excessive inspections, targeting, improper timing, disregarding reasonable rescheduling requests, recording beyond a lawful inspection's scope or misrepresenting entry reasons. Owner includes lessors, sublessors, successors and authorized representatives. Access rights incorporate Civil Code section 1954 or other applicable law; outside-normal-business-hours entry has exceptions for health and safety or tenant agreement, and recording restrictions concern portions beyond lawful entry or inspection. The verbal-abuse prohibition concerns offensive words inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction, including written and electronic communications. Section 8-3120(e)'s exemptions and 30-day threshold are not expressly extended to this separate anti-harassment provision; provision-specific Rental Unit definitions and Article exemptions require review.

rules.title: Baseless eviction, property removal and false protection information
rules.requirement: Covered actors may not pursue termination on facts the owner lacks reasonable cause to believe or untenable legal theories, remove tenant property without prior written consent except in enforcing a legal termination, or give false tenant-protection information, including the specified misleading lease-language and repayment-plan demands. Liability under the baseless-possession-action provision requires the tenant first to obtain a favorable termination of that action.

rules.title: Buyout pressure, quiet enjoyment and organizing protections
rules.requirement: Covered actors may not make more than one payment-to-vacate offer in six months after a tenant's written refusal of further offers, use threatening buyout pressure, use another language to intimidate or deceive, interfere with quiet enjoyment, repeatedly disturb occupancy to induce departure or waiver, or remove services to cause departure. rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to an Owner or person acting as principal or agent offering Santa Ana Residential Real Property for rent, or an owner's contractor, subcontractor or employee, regarding property under a rental agreement, other tenancy or estate at will however created. rules.title: Complete registration required before eviction
rules.requirement: A landlord may not evict a tenant from a covered Rental Unit unless its registration is complete and accurate.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to a Landlord, including an owner, lessor, sublessor, successor or representative authorized to bind the landlord, evicting from a Santa Ana Rental Unit subject to Article XIX's Registry requirements. Complete registration requires payment of all City fees and penalties and a complete, accurate form containing information required by Division 4 and implementing policies. Annual exemption declarations and supporting documents are required under section 8-3160(d), with a stated consequence of deemed Article coverage for failure to submit by July 1 and possible retroactive revocation for affirmative misrepresentation. Section 8-3120(e) termination exemptions and section 8-3147 rent exemptions are provision-specific and do not by themselves establish exemption from Registry duties. Their interaction, the Rental Unit definition and the stated October 1, 2023 enforcement commencement require execution review.
rules.quoted_span:
Furthermore, no Landlord shall
advertise for rent, demand or accept Rent for a Rental Unit, or evict any Tenant from a
Rental Unit, if the Rental Unit Registration is not complete and accurate.

rules.title: Formal application before criminal-history inquiry
rules.requirement: Inquiry into and consideration of an applicant's criminal history must wait until submission of a formal application containing all required review materials or information. A landlord or real estate broker may discuss criminal history disclosed through the applicant's unsolicited voluntary written or oral disclosure.
rules.key_value: After formal application
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, and real estate brokers as defined in that section, in connection with residential rentals, leases and subleases and applicants seeking those transactions or related information. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Article prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits consideration of criminal history, but only for the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, or to property designated by the landlord or broker to participate in a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly. The unsolicited voluntary disclosure exception permits discussion of the history disclosed.
rules.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application. Notwithstanding the foregoing, if the applicant discloses any information regarding his or her criminal history by unsolicited voluntary written or oral disclosure, the landlord or real estate broker may discuss the criminal history disclosed by the applicant.

rules.title: Written notification before criminal-history inquiry
rules.requirement: Before a criminal-history inquiry, the landlord or broker must give standard written notification explaining written consent, at least three business days after receipt of notice to submit evidence upon consenting, and the right to obtain inquiry results on request, with the Appendix A housing information form attached. The landlord or broker may hold the unit for rehabilitation information but need not hold it after an initial eligibility determination.
rules.key_value: At least 3 business days to submit evidence
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies before a criminal-history inquiry by a landlord as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, or by a real estate broker as defined in that section, concerning an applicant for a residential rental, lease or sublease. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Section 2:31-8 exempts Article prohibitions where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, and for property designated by the landlord or broker for a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly; whether those exemptions from prohibitions also displace this affirmative notification duty requires review.
rules.quoted_span:
Prior to conducting any criminal history inquiry regarding an applicant, the landlord or real estate broker shall provide standard written notification to the applicant.

1.

Advising that, upon the written consent of the applicant, the landlord or real estate broker will conduct a criminal history inquiry;

2.
Advising that upon consenting to a criminal history inquiry, the applicant has the right and opportunity of not less than three business days from the receipt of notice to submit evidence which may inform the consideration under Section 2:31-4 of this Article; and

3.

Advising that the applicant has the right to receive a copy, upon the applicant's request, of the results of any criminal history inquiry obtained regarding the applicant.

4.
Attaching a copy of the Information Form Regarding Criminal Record Review - Housing, attached hereto as Appendix A.

c.

A landlord or real estate broker may hold a housing unit open until an applicant provides information about rehabilitation, but a landlord or real estate broker is not required to hold a housing unit after making an initial determination of an applicant's eligibility.

rules.title: Criminal records excluded from inquiry and adverse action
rules.requirement: A landlord or broker must not inquire into, require disclosure of, or take adverse action based on arrests or accusations that are neither pending nor resulted in conviction; erased, expunged, pardoned or otherwise legally nullified records; juvenile delinquency adjudications; or sealed records.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, and real estate brokers as defined in that section, in connection with residential rentals, leases and subleases. The prohibition protects any person described in § 2:31-3(d). Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Article prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits consideration of criminal history, but only for the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, or to property designated by the landlord or broker to participate in a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall not be permissible for a landlord or real estate broker to conduct any criminal history inquiry, require any person to disclose or reveal, or to take any adverse action against any person on the basis of

1.

Any arrest or criminal accusation made against such person which is not then pending against that person and which did not result in a conviction;

2.

Any records which have been erased, expunged, the subject of an executive pardon, or otherwise legally nullified; or
3.

Any juvenile adjudications of delinquency or any records which have been sealed.

rules.title: Required individualized criminal-history considerations
rules.requirement: When evaluating an applicant and a criminal-history inquiry conducted within § 2:31-3's limits, the landlord or broker must consider any supplied rehabilitation, good-conduct or record-accuracy information, including rehabilitation certificates. The evaluation must also consider time since conviction or release and the nature and circumstances of the crimes.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, and real estate brokers as defined in that section, evaluating applicants and criminal-history inquiry results in connection with residential rentals, leases, assignments or subleases. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Section 2:31-8 exempts Article prohibitions where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, and for property designated by the landlord or broker for a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly; whether those exemptions from prohibitions also displace this affirmative consideration duty requires review.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord or real estate broker shall consider the following factors in evaluating the applicant and the results of any criminal history inquiry, conducted in accordance with the limitations of Section 2:31-3 .

1.
Any information, if provided, pertaining to the degree of rehabilitation and good conduct or to the accuracy of the criminal record in question produced by the applicant, or produced on his or her behalf to the landlord or real estate broker, including but not limited to any certificate of rehabilitation issued by any state or federal agency, which includes but is not limited to certificates issued pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2A:168A-1 to 16;

2.
The amount of time that has passed since the conviction(s) and/or release from custody; and

3.

The nature of and circumstances surrounding the crime(s).

rules.title: Notice and inquiry results after an adverse decision
rules.requirement: Within 10 business days after a final adverse determination following a criminal-history inquiry that results in refusal of a rental, lease, assignment or sublease, the landlord or broker must provide written notice stating the reasons and consideration of § 2:31-4 factors, plus a copy of the inquiry results. All required documents and notices must be sent together in one registered mailing.
rules.key_value: 10 business days; one registered mailing
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a landlord as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, or a real estate broker as defined in that section, conducts a criminal-history inquiry and then makes a final adverse determination refusing an applicant a residential rental, lease, assignment or sublease. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Section 2:31-8 exempts Article prohibitions where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, and for property designated by the landlord or broker for a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly; whether those exemptions from prohibitions also displace this affirmative notice duty requires review.
rules.quoted_span:
If after conducting a criminal history inquiry the landlord or real estate broker makes a final determination adverse to the applicant resulting in the refusal of any rental, lease, assignment, or sublease, the landlord or real estate broker shall, within 10 business days.

1.

Notify the applicant in writing of the adverse action, stating the reasons for rejection and including the landlord's or real estate broker's consideration of factors required under Section 2:31-4 of this Article; and
2.

Provide the applicant with a copy of the results of the criminal history inquiry.

b.

A copy of all documents and notices required under Section 2:31-5a shall be sent in one mailing, by registered mail, to the applicant.

rules.title: Confidentiality and restricted use of criminal history
rules.requirement: Criminal-history information obtained in the rental, lease or sublease process must remain confidential and be shared only with individuals needing it to evaluate applicants consistently with the Article. Landlords and brokers may use or distribute it only for Article purposes and may not disseminate it to other entities or individuals except as dictated by law.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to applicants' criminal-history information obtained in connection with residential rentals, leases or subleases, including its handling by landlords as defined in § 2:31-1, meaning owners, lessees, sublessees, assignees, managing agents, other persons entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employees or agents, and real estate brokers as defined in that section. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Article prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, or to property designated by the landlord or broker for a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly. Section 2:31-6 permits sharing for consistent applicant evaluation on a need-to-know basis and dissemination to others as dictated by law; the reach of § 2:31-8's exemption from prohibitions into affirmative confidentiality duties requires review.
rules.quoted_span:
Any information pertaining to an applicant's criminal history obtained in conjunction with the rental, lease, or sublease process:

1.

Shall remain confidential;

2.

Shall only be shared with individuals who have a need to know for the purpose of evaluating applicants in a manner consistent with this Article;

3.

Shall not be used, distributed, or disseminated by the landlord or real estate broker for any use other than those described in this Article; and

4.
Shall not be used, distributed, or disseminated by the landlord or real estate broker to any other entity or individual, except as dictated by law.

rules.title: Restrictions on criminal-history advertising
rules.requirement: A landlord or broker must not produce or disseminate rental advertisements directly or indirectly referencing use or consideration of criminal history, except expressions of eligibility restrictions under § 2:31-8(a) limited to legally specified offenses and time periods. In an action under this section, such an advertisement is presumptive evidence that the landlord or broker authorized it.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords as defined in § 2:31-1, including an owner, lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, other person entitled to rent, lease or sublease the property, or their employee or agent, and real estate brokers as defined in that section, producing or disseminating advertisements connected to residential rentals, leases or subleases. Advertisements include circulation, mailing, posting or other publication in any media promoting the landlord or broker or alerting audiences or prospective applicants to property availability. Excludes rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling when the other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence or by the owner's family household at the time of rental; also excludes rental of rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied by that person as a residence or by that person's family household at the time of rental. Article prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits criminal-history consideration, limited to the specified offenses or offense types and time periods, or to property designated by the landlord or broker for a federal, state or local government program or obligation designed to encourage housing for individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions must be interpreted narrowly. Section 2:31-7 expressly allows expression of statutory, regulatory or rule-based eligibility restrictions described in § 2:31-8(a) only within the offenses and time periods established by law.
rules.quoted_span:
In connection with any rental, lease, or sublease, it shall be unlawful for a landlord or real estate broker to produce or disseminate any advertisement that directly or indirectly references the use or consideration of an applicant's criminal history, except that nothing in this section shall preclude the expression of statutory, regulatory, or rule-based eligibility restrictions applicable to the rental, lease or sublease of real property as described in Section 2:31-8a so long as such expression is limited to the specified offense(s) and time period(s) as established by law.
b.

In any action against any landlord or real estate broker under this section, any such advertisement shall be presumptive evidence that the landlord or real estate broker authorized the advertisement.

rules.title: Nondiscrimination in access to rental housing
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers must not discriminate on protected grounds when allowing applicants to view or rent an apartment, subject to the exemption for owner-occupied two-family dwellings.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords, sellers and rental agents involved in residential apartment viewing or rental transactions in Cambridge, except two-family dwellings where the owner lives. Protected grounds identified by the source are disability, race, color, national origin or ancestry, family status, source of income including Section 8 and public benefits, marital status including married and non-married individuals, sex including allegations of sexual harassment, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, age, religious creed, military status, relationship status and family structure. The source defines disability consistently with the ADA as a physical or mental impairment substantially limiting one or more major life activities. The supplied vocabulary cannot fully represent the covered actors and transactions.
rules.exemptions: Two-family dwellings where the owner lives.
rules.quoted_span:
The Fair Housing Ordinance prohibits discrimination in real estate transactions such as:
viewing or renting an apartment
terms and conditions of tenancy
refusing to reasonably accommodate a person with a  disability if the accommodation would not cause an undue hardship to the landlord
viewing or purchasing a home
applying for or obtaining a mortgage
purchasing homeowners' or renters' insurance
printing, publicizing or advertising housing in a discriminatory manner
Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants. Tenant selection may be based on:
an applicant's ability to pay the rent
an applicant's ability to take care of the apartment and to respect the rights of others
NOTE: there is an exemption for 2-family dwellings, when the owner lives there

rules.title: Reasonable and uniformly applied tenant-selection standards
rules.requirement: Landlords, sellers and rental agents must use reasonable applicant-selection standards and apply them equally and uniformly to all applicants, except at owner-occupied two-family dwellings. Permitted tenant-selection considerations include ability to pay rent, care for the apartment and respect others' rights.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords, sellers and rental agents selecting applicants for residential rental housing in Cambridge. Two-family dwellings where the owner lives are exempt. The supplied fact vocabulary cannot establish whether the person conducting selection is a landlord, seller or rental agent; the fee-charger role fields do not establish those roles for tenant selection.
rules.exemptions: Two-family dwellings where the owner lives.

rules.title: Reasonable disability accommodation in rental access
rules.requirement: In covered residential rental transactions, landlords must not refuse a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability when it would not cause the landlord undue hardship. Owner-occupied two-family dwellings are exempt.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to landlords in Cambridge residential rental transactions involving a person with a disability, including access to viewing or renting an apartment. Disability means a physical or mental impairment substantially limiting one or more major life activities, defined consistently with the ADA. The accommodation must be reasonable and must not cause undue hardship to the landlord; two-family dwellings where the owner lives are exempt. The supplied vocabulary cannot fully express landlord status, disability, accommodation reasonableness or undue hardship.
rules.exemptions: Two-family dwellings where the owner lives; the stated accommodation obligation is conditional on the accommodation not causing undue hardship to the landlord.

rules.title: Annual gross rent increase limit
rules.requirement: An owner of covered residential real property must limit increases over any 12-month period to the lesser of 5 percent plus the statutory percentage change in the cost of living or 10 percent of the lowest gross rent charged during the 12 months before the increase takes effect. Owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions and credits accepted by the tenant are excluded when determining that lowest gross rent.
rules.key_value: Lesser of 5% plus statutory CPI change or 10% in any 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks. Exclude: housing restricted by deed, a regulatory restriction in a government-agency agreement, or another recorded document as affordable housing for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons and families under Health and Safety Code Section 50093, or subject to an agreement providing affordable-housing subsidies for those groups under that section or comparable federal statutes; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or kindergarten-through-grade-12 schools; housing under valid public rent or price control consistent with Chapter 2.7 that limits annual increases below subdivision (a); non-mobilehome housing issued an occupancy certificate within the previous 15 years; separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, whose owner is neither a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, nor mobilehome-park management under Section 798.2, but only if tenants received the exact subdivision (d)(5)(B) written exemption notice in the required form and location; and property with two separate units in one structure, neither an ADU nor junior ADU, where the owner occupied one as the owner's principal residence at tenancy inception and continues occupying it. For the separately alienable exemption, the notice must be in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes; earlier existing tenancies may receive it outside the agreement. Subdivision (j) excludes a mobilehome homeowner as defined in Section 798.9; that definition is not supplied and requires review. For a new tenancy with no prior tenant remaining in lawful possession, the initial rental rate is outside subdivision (a); subsequent increases are covered.
rules.exemptions: All address and tenancy exceptions are preserved in coverage_conditions. Owner includes a person acting as principal or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent, and a predecessor in interest. The cost-of-living change uses the applicable metropolitan CPI-U, or California CPI-U where no metropolitan CPI-U is published, with the statutory successor and newly published index provisions. Before August 1, compare April of the preceding year with April of the year before that; on or after August 1, compare April of the current year with April of the preceding year. Use the corresponding March comparison if no April amount is published for the applicable area, and round the percentage change to the nearest one-tenth of 1 percent.
rules.quoted_span:
(a) (1)   Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase. In determining the lowest gross rental amount pursuant to this section, any rent discounts, incentives, concessions, or credits offered by the owner of such unit of residential real property and accepted by the tenant shall be excluded. The gross per-month rental rate and any owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions, or credits shall be separately listed and identified in the lease or rental agreement or any
amendments to an existing lease or rental agreement.

(2) If the same tenant remains in occupancy of a unit of residential real property over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate for the unit of residential real property shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period, subject to the other restrictions of this subdivision governing gross rental rate increase.

rules.title: Civil remedies and public enforcement
rules.requirement: An owner demanding, accepting, receiving or retaining rent above the section's maximum is liable in a civil action to the tenant from whom payment is demanded, accepted, received or retained for injunctive relief, the excess amount, discretionary reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and, upon a showing of willfulness or oppression, fraud or malice, damages up to three times the excess amount. The Attorney General and the rental unit's city attorney or county counsel may enforce the section and seek injunctions in the respective public entity's name; subdivision (k) injunction actions presume irreparable harm to a tenant, and subdivision (k) actions must be brought within three years after accrual.
rules.key_value: Excess-rent damages; conditional damages up to 3 times the excess; 3-year filing limit
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks. Exclude: housing restricted by deed, a regulatory restriction in a government-agency agreement, or another recorded document as affordable housing for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons and families under Health and Safety Code Section 50093, or subject to an agreement providing affordable-housing subsidies for those groups under that section or comparable federal statutes; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or kindergarten-through-grade-12 schools; housing under valid public rent or price control consistent with Chapter 2.7 that limits annual increases below subdivision (a); non-mobilehome housing issued an occupancy certificate within the previous 15 years; separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, whose owner is neither a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, nor mobilehome-park management under Section 798.2, but only if tenants received the exact subdivision (d)(5)(B) written exemption notice in the required form and location; and property with two separate units in one structure, neither an ADU nor junior ADU, where the owner occupied one as the owner's principal residence at tenancy inception and continues occupying it. Subdivision (j) excludes a mobilehome homeowner as defined in Section 798.9; that definition is not supplied and requires review. Address coverage does not establish an excessive rent payment, actionable demand, culpable state of mind, timely claim or entitled plaintiff.
rules.exemptions: All address and tenancy exceptions are preserved in coverage_conditions. Owner includes a person acting as principal or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent, and a predecessor in interest. Initial rates allowed by subdivision (b) are not capped by subdivision (a). Subdivisions (h)(2) and (i)(2) expressly preclude liability for corresponding historical overpayments associated with their specified rollback periods; the historical provisions and their relationship to a claim require review. The source measures damages by excess payment amounts and supplies no separate fixed per-violation penalty.
rules.quoted_span:
(k) (1) An owner who demands, accepts, receives, or retains any payment of rent in excess of the maximum rent allowed by this section shall be liable in a civil action to the tenant from whom those payments are demanded, accepted, received, or retained for all of the following:
(A) Injunctive relief.
(B) Damages in the amount by which any payment demanded, accepted, received, or retained exceeds the
maximum allowable rent.
(C) In the court’s discretion, reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.
(D) Upon a showing that the owner has acted willfully or with oppression, fraud, or malice, damages up to three times the amount by which any payment demanded, accepted, received, or retained exceeds the maximum allowable rent.
(2) The Attorney General, in the name of the people of the State of California, and the city attorney or county counsel in the jurisdiction in which the rental unit is located, in the name of the city or county, may do both of the following:
(A) Enforce the provisions of this section.
(B) Seek injunctive relief based on violations of this section.
(3) In an action pursuant to this
subdivision for injunctive relief, it shall be presumed that a tenant suffers irreparable harm through violation of this section.
(4) An action pursuant to this subdivision shall not be brought after the date that is three years from the date on which the cause of action accrued.

rules.title: Prohibition on selling or using defined algorithmic rental devices
rules.requirement: Entities may not sell or use defined algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action if they believe an entity violates the law.
rules.exemptions: The regulated term “algorithmic device” means a device, such as a software program, that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purpose of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit.
rules.quoted_span:
Legislation
adding Section 37.10C to the Rent Ordinance went into effect on October 14, 2024. The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
The term “algorithmic device” means a device such as a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purposes of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit. The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.

rules.title: Annual allowable rent increase for March 2026–February 2027
rules.requirement: For rent-controlled units, landlords must use an annual allowable increase of 1.6% of the tenant's base rent for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
rules.key_value: 1.6% of tenant's base rent
rules.exemptions: Limited to rent-controlled units; the announcement does not define which units are rent-controlled.
rules.citation: San Francisco Rent Board, Annual Rent Increase for 3/1/26 - 2/28/27 Announced, January 14, 2026
rules.quoted_span:
For
rent-controlled units
, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
To calculate the dollar amount of the 1.6% annual rent increase, multiply the tenant's base rent by .016. For example, if the tenant's base rent is $2,000.00, the annual increase would be calculated as follows: $2,000.00 x .016 = $32.00. The tenant's new base rent would be $2,032.00 ($2,000.00 + $32.00).

rules.title: Just cause must be the dominant eviction motive
rules.requirement: A landlord evicting a tenant covered by the Rent Ordinance's eviction provisions must have one of the 17 specified just-cause reasons as the dominant motive; mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not suffice. A landlord who unlawfully evicts or attempts to evict a tenant may face substantial civil and/or criminal liability.
rules.key_value: 17 specified just-cause grounds
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental tenancies covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's eviction provisions. Coverage includes tenancies in newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, and some tenancies whose rent is regulated by another government agency, even when exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limitations. The source does not fully define covered rental tenancies, enumerate eviction exemptions, or identify which tenancies regulated by another government agency are included; those address-level eligibility questions require review.
rules.exemptions: The summarized grounds are: nonpayment, habitual late payment, or frequent bounced checks; failure to cure a substantial lease breach; nuisance or substantial interference with the landlord's or other tenants' comfort, safety, or enjoyment that is severe, continuing, or reoccurring; illegal use, excluding mere occupancy of an unwarranted unit and a single Chapter 41A short-term rental violation cured within 30 days of the landlord's written notice; refusal after written request to renew an expired agreement for a like term on materially the same terms; refusal after written notice to cease to permit legally required landlord access; an unapproved subtenant being the only tenant remaining at the agreement's end, with approval potentially oral or implied by the landlord's conduct; owner occupancy or, in limited circumstances, occupancy by immediate family; good-faith recovery to sell pursuant to an approved condominium conversion; demolition or permanent removal of an individual unit from housing use; capital improvements or rehabilitation temporarily making the unit uninhabitable, with immediate reoccupancy after completion; substantial rehabilitation of an essentially uninhabitable building at least 50 years old, with proposed work costing at least 75% of new construction; withdrawal of all building rental units under the Ellis Act; lead remediation or abatement required by Health Code Articles 11 or 26; demolition or permanent removal pursuant to a City development agreement under Administrative Code Chapter 56; expiration of a Good Samaritan occupancy agreement with eviction notice served within 60 days after expiration, where the tenancy provides a reduced-rent temporary replacement unit to a tenant displaced by emergency or disaster; and completion of a development project requiring demolition under Planning Code Section 317. The source does not detail the limited circumstances permitting immediate-family occupancy or all requirements of the referenced grounds. Exemption from rent increase limitations does not itself establish exemption from eviction protections.

rules.title: Just cause for removal of housing services
rules.requirement: A landlord must have a just-cause reason to take away or remove access to covered housing services, including garage facilities, parking facilities, driveways, storage spaces, and laundry rooms. A landlord complying with Ordinance Section 37.2(r) may temporarily remove certain services, including parking and storage, to perform mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work required by the Building Code.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies within the source's discussion of rental tenancies covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's eviction provisions. Those protections can include newly constructed units first receiving a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for Costa-Hawkins rent increases, and some tenancies with rent regulated by another government agency despite exemption from rent increase limits. The source does not fully specify tenancy coverage or exemptions, identify the included government-regulated tenancies, or establish whether the housing-services provision has any additional address-level limitations. These eligibility questions require review.
rules.exemptions: The service list is nonexclusive. Temporary removal of certain housing services for mandatory Building Code soft-story seismic retrofit work is permitted only when the landlord has complied with Ordinance Section 37.2(r); the source does not reproduce those requirements or fully identify the services eligible for this exception.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord also needs a "just cause“ reason to take away or remove access to certain
housing services
, including but not limited to garage facilities, parking facilities, driveways, storage spaces, and laundry rooms. However, a landlord who has complied with the requirements of Ordinance Section 37.2(r) may
temporarily remove certain housing services
, including parking and storage spaces, in order to perform mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work required by
the Building Code
.
Some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limitations of the Ordinance are still subject to the eviction provisions of the Ordinance, and tenants in these categories can only be evicted for one of the “just cause” reasons listed in the Ordinance. This includes tenancies in newly constructed rental units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies that are eligible for a rent increase under the

rules.title: Immediate reoccupancy after temporary displacement for work
rules.requirement: When a landlord recovers possession for capital improvements or rehabilitation work that makes a covered rental unit temporarily uninhabitable, the landlord must allow the tenant to reoccupy the unit immediately after the work is completed.
rules.key_value: Immediately after work is completed
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental tenancies covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's eviction provisions. The source includes newly constructed units first receiving a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for Costa-Hawkins rent increases, and some tenancies with rent regulated by another government agency despite exemption from rent increase limits. It does not fully define tenancy coverage, enumerate eviction exemptions, or identify the included government-regulated tenancies; those address-level eligibility questions require review.
rules.exemptions: This reoccupancy duty is stated for capital improvements or rehabilitation that temporarily makes the unit uninhabitable. The source separately lists substantial rehabilitation of an essentially uninhabitable building at least 50 years old with proposed work costing at least 75% of new construction; it does not expressly extend this reoccupancy duty to that separate ground or to permanent removal from housing use.

rules.title: Application screening fee cost and inflation-adjusted limits
rules.requirement: An owner of residential rental property or their agent charging an application screening fee must limit it to actual out-of-pocket information-gathering costs plus the reasonable value of time spent obtaining applicant information. The fee also must not exceed $30 per applicant, subject to annual adjustments commensurate with increases in the Consumer Price Index beginning January 1, 1998.
rules.key_value: Actual costs plus reasonable time value, capped at $30 per applicant with permitted annual CPI adjustments beginning January 1, 1998
rules.exemptions: An application screening fee is a nonrefundable monetary payment charged by the landlord or their agent to purchase a consumer credit report and validate, review, or otherwise process a residential rental application. Applicant includes an entity or individual requesting a residential unit or agreeing to act as a guarantor or cosignor. Accepting and relying on an applicant-provided consumer credit report is optional; the section also permits accepting a reusable screening report pursuant to Section 1950.1. Charging a fee remains subject to subdivision (c).
rules.quoted_span:
(a) Notwithstanding Section 1950.5, when a landlord or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, the landlord or their agent may charge, pursuant to subdivision (c), that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant. The information requested and obtained by the landlord or their agent may include, but is not limited to, personal reference checks and consumer credit reports produced by consumer credit reporting agencies as defined in Section 1785.3. A landlord or their agent may, but is not required to, accept and rely upon a consumer credit report presented by an applicant.
(b) The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual
out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.title: No screening fee when no unit is reasonably available
rules.requirement: An owner of residential rental property or their agent must not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available then or will be available within a reasonable period.
rules.exemptions: The prohibition depends on actual or constructive knowledge of unit availability. Application screening fee means the defined nonrefundable monetary payment to purchase a consumer credit report and validate, review, or otherwise process a residential rental application; applicant includes entities and individuals requesting a unit and those agreeing to act as guarantors or cosignors.
rules.quoted_span: (c) (1) A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time.

rules.title: Required alternative screening processes for fee collection
rules.requirement: An owner of residential rental property or their agent may collect an application screening fee only if, at collection, they offer either the ordered-consideration process with written criteria, first-qualified approval and consideration-linked charging, or the process refunding every unselected applicant's entire fee. The first process requires correction of qualifying inadvertent charges within seven days, subject to the applicant's discretionary alternative credit, while the second requires refunds by the earlier of seven days after selecting a tenant or 30 days after application submission.
rules.key_value: Two permitted processes; seven-day inadvertent-charge refund or unselected-applicant refund by the earlier of seven days after selection and 30 days after submission
rules.exemptions: Under subdivision (c)(2)(A), completed applications must be considered in receipt order under the landlord's established screening criteria; those criteria must accompany the application form in writing; the first applicant meeting them must be approved; and a fee may not be charged unless or until the application is actually considered. Inadvertent collection caused by multiple concurrent submissions does not violate the consideration-linked charging rule if an unconsidered applicant receives a refund within seven days. The landlord may instead offer, solely at the applicant's discretion, to apply that fee to another rental unit offered by the landlord. This process does not require refunding a fee when an application is considered and denied for failure to meet the established criteria. Under subdivision (c)(2)(B), every unselected applicant receives the entire fee back regardless of the reason. Application screening fee means the defined nonrefundable monetary payment to purchase a consumer credit report and validate, review, or otherwise process a residential rental application. Applicant includes entities and individuals requesting a unit or agreeing to act as guarantors or cosignors.
rules.quoted_span:
(2) A landlord or their agent may charge an applicant an application screening fee only if the landlord or their agent, at the time the application screening fee is collected, offers any of the following:
(A) An application screening process that complies with all of the following:
(i) Completed applications are considered, as provided for in the landlord’s established screening criteria, in the order in which the completed applications were received. The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form.
(ii) The first applicant who meets the landlord’s established screening criteria is approved for tenancy.
(iii) Applicants are not
charged an application screening fee unless or until their application is actually considered.
(iv) Clause (iii) shall not be considered violated if a landlord or their agent inadvertently collects an application screening fee from an applicant as the result of multiple concurrent application submissions, provided that the landlord or their agent issues a refund of the application screening fee within seven days to any applicant whose application is not considered. The landlord may offer, as an alternative to refunding the screening fee, the option, at the applicant’s discretion, for the screening fee paid by the applicant to be applied to an application for another rental unit offered by the landlord. A landlord or their agent shall not be required to refund an application screening fee to an applicant whose application is denied, after consideration, because the applicant does not meet the landlord’s established screening criteria.
(B) An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.
(d) The landlord or their agent shall provide, personally, or by mail, the applicant with a receipt for the fee paid by the applicant, which receipt shall itemize the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord or their agent to obtain and process the information about the applicant. The landlord or their agent and the applicant may agree to have the landlord provide a copy of the receipt for the fee paid by the applicant to an email account provided by the applicant.
(e) If the landlord or their agent does
not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, the landlord or their agent shall return any amount of the screening fee that is not used for the purposes authorized by this section to the applicant.
(f) If an application screening fee has been paid by the applicant, the landlord or their agent shall provide a copy of the consumer credit report to the applicant who is the subject of that report by personal delivery, mail, or email within seven days of the landlord or their agent receiving the report.
(g) Nothing in this section prevents a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report pursuant to Section 1950.1.
(h) As used in this section, “landlord” means an owner of residential rental property.
(i) As used in
this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property.
(j) As used in this section, “applicant” means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or their agent to rent a residential housing unit, or an entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement.
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.
(l) This section is not intended
to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
