rules.title: Just cause required to terminate a covered tenancy
rules.requirement: A landlord may terminate a covered tenancy only for a specified at-fault cause or a specified no-fault cause pursued in good faith. Each ground remains subject to its statutory qualifications and the applicable notice, cure, relocation, and other termination requirements.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, where a natural-person tenant has a lawful right to continuous use or occupancy for more than 30 days; a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including extensions or renewals of three months or less, is excluded. Apply every section 98.0703 exemption: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code section 1940(b); short-term residential occupancy defined by and subject to Code Chapter 5, Article 10, Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement, or other document as affordable to very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing, except Section 8 tenant-based assistance; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned and operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution; a tenant sharing a bathroom or kitchen with a landlord whose principal residence is the property; a landlord-principal-residence single-family residence, including the stated no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and a mobilehome; two separate dwelling units in one structure where the landlord occupies one as a principal residence at tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless it is a mobilehome; and separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, only when the landlord is neither a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, nor mobilehome-park management, and tenants receive the prescribed written exemption notice. That notice must be in the lease for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after January 1, 2024; it may be in the lease for earlier tenancies. Nonprofit transitional housing means nonprofit-operated temporary housing for up to 24 months with supportive services directed toward permanent housing. Exact institutional definitions, ownership circumstances, principal-residence timing, and notice requirements require execution review.
rules.exemptions: The landlord definition includes an owner, a person acting as principal or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent, and a predecessor in interest. At-fault grounds are rent default; material lease breach as described in Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3), including violation after written corrective notice; statutory nuisance or waste; refusal after written request to renew a written lease that terminated on or after June 24, 2023 for a substantially similar duration and provisions that comply with law; tenant criminal activity on the property or its common areas; a Penal Code section 422(a) criminal threat against the landlord or another tenant regardless of location; prohibited assignment or subletting; refusal of legally authorized entry; unlawful use; failure by a former employee, agent, or licensee to vacate after termination of that status; or failure to surrender possession following the specified written tenant notice or an offer accepted by the landlord in writing. No-fault grounds require honest intent without ulterior motives and are qualified owner/family occupancy, withdrawal from the rental market, specified government/court orders or a local ordinance requiring vacancy, or qualified demolition/substantial remodeling. A habitability order requiring vacancy for fewer than 30 days is not just cause. Owner occupancy and remodeling are subject to the detailed restrictions in section 98.0704(b)(1) and (4).
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this 
Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.

rules.title: Conditions and remedies for owner or family occupancy termination
rules.requirement: An owner invoking owner or family occupancy must satisfy the ownership, lease, vacancy, notice, proof, and good-faith conditions, with the intended occupant moving in within 90 days after the tenant vacates and residing there as a primary residence for at least 12 continuous months. If the occupancy requirements fail, the owner must offer the displaced tenant the same rent and lease terms and reimburse reasonable moving expenses exceeding relocation assistance already paid, subject to the stated death exception.
rules.key_value: Move in within 90 days; occupy for at least 12 continuous months
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, under a lawful natural-person tenancy for continuous use or occupancy exceeding 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and their extensions or renewals of three months or less. Exclude every section 98.0703 circumstance: statutory transient/tourist hotels; locally defined short-term residential occupancy; document-restricted affordable housing for very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing other than Section 8 tenant-based assistance; Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious-facility, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care, adult residential-facility, and nonprofit transitional housing; institution-owned-and-operated higher-education or K–12 dormitories; bathroom/kitchen sharing with a principal-resident landlord; landlord-principal-residence single-family housing, including the specified no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and mobilehomes; a two-unit single structure with a landlord occupying one unit as a principal residence from tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; and separately alienable housing whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management and whose tenants received the prescribed written exemption notice, in the lease for commencement or renewal on or after January 1, 2024. Nonprofit transitional housing is nonprofit-operated temporary housing up to 24 months with supportive services aimed at permanent housing. For this owner-occupancy ground, preserve the section 98.0702 natural-person, family-trust, recorded-interest, related-owner, and LLC/partnership ownership qualifications. The ground is unavailable if the intended occupant already occupies a rental unit on the property or a similar unit is vacant there. For leases entered on or after June 24, 2023, the tenant must agree to termination in writing or the lease must expressly authorize the specified owner/family occupancy termination. These ownership, vacancy, lease-date, and institutional qualifications cannot be completely represented with the allowed facts.
rules.exemptions: The intended occupant must be the owner or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, child by blood or adoption, grandchild by blood or adoption, parent, or grandparent. Good faith means honest intent without ulterior motives. An owner is a natural person with at least a 25 percent recorded interest; a natural person with any recorded interest when all recorded ownership is divided among the specified related owners; or a natural person whose recorded interest is owned through an LLC or partnership. Natural person includes a settlor or beneficiary of a defined family trust and, for LLC or partnership ownership, a natural person with a 25 percent ownership interest; the interaction of these definitions requires review. The termination notice must name the intended occupants, state their relationship to the owner, and advise that proof may be requested; the owner must provide proof on request, potentially including non-public documents. For pre-June 24, 2023 tenancies, adding the specified owner-occupancy termination provision is a substantially similar provision for section 98.0704(a)(5). Timely move-in followed by the intended occupant's death before completing 12 months of primary residence is not noncompliance with this ground.

rules.title: Demolition and substantial-remodel termination safeguards
rules.requirement: A landlord pursuing a good-faith demolition or qualifying substantial-remodel termination must satisfy the work and vacancy restrictions, post required permit applications within three business days, obtain required permits before notice, and provide the specified termination notice certified under penalty of perjury. rules.key_value: At least 30 continuous days of necessary vacancy for substantial remodeling
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, under a lawful natural-person tenancy for continuous use or occupancy exceeding 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and their extensions or renewals of three months or less. Exclude every section 98.0703 circumstance: statutory transient/tourist hotels; locally defined short-term residential occupancy; document-restricted affordable housing for very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing other than Section 8 tenant-based assistance; Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious-facility, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care, adult residential-facility, and nonprofit transitional housing; institution-owned-and-operated higher-education or K–12 dormitories; bathroom/kitchen sharing with a principal-resident landlord; landlord-principal-residence single-family housing, including the specified no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and mobilehomes; a two-unit single structure with a landlord occupying one unit as a principal residence from tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; and separately alienable housing whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management and whose tenants received the prescribed written exemption notice, in the lease for commencement or renewal on or after January 1, 2024. rules.exemptions: Substantial remodeling means permit-requiring replacement or substantial modification of structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical systems, or legally compliant abatement of hazardous materials including lead-based paint, mold, or asbestos; the work must be unsafe to accomplish reasonably with the tenant present and require at least 30 continuous days of vacancy. Cosmetic work alone and work safely performed without vacancy do not qualify, and the tenant need not vacate on days continued occupancy would comply with health, safety, and habitability law. Notice must state the intent, describe work and expected duration or demolition date, explain necessary vacancy, include permits or, solely for permit-free hazardous-material abatement, the signed contractor agreement reasonably detailing the work, and include section 98.0706(b)(1)(C)'s reoffer-right notification. Permit posting and advance procurement apply when permits are required.

rules.title: Tenant-protection notice and guide
rules.requirement: A covered landlord must give tenants the prescribed protection notice in at least 12-point font, comply with Civil Code section 1632, and include the Tenant Protection Guide according to the tenancy-specific delivery rules. The San Diego Housing Commission must prepare the guide and make it available on its website.

rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, under a lawful natural-person tenancy for continuous use or occupancy exceeding 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and their extensions or renewals of three months or less. Exclude every section 98.0703 circumstance: statutory transient/tourist hotels; locally defined short-term residential occupancy; document-restricted affordable housing for very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing other than Section 8 tenant-based assistance; Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious-facility, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care, adult residential-facility, and nonprofit transitional housing; institution-owned-and-operated higher-education or K–12 dormitories; bathroom/kitchen sharing with a principal-resident landlord; landlord-principal-residence single-family housing, including the specified no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and mobilehomes; a two-unit single structure with a landlord occupying one unit as a principal residence from tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; and separately alienable housing whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management and whose tenants received the prescribed written exemption notice, in the lease for commencement or renewal on or after January 1, 2024. Nonprofit transitional housing is nonprofit-operated temporary housing up to 24 months with supportive services aimed at permanent housing. Preserve whether the tenancy existed before June 24, 2023 or commenced or renewed on or after that date, because the delivery requirements differ. rules.title: No-fault notice and relocation assistance
rules.requirement: For a no-fault termination, the landlord must give the specified notice in at least 12-point font at least 30 or 60 days before termination as required by Civil Code section 1946.1, and provide two months of actual lease rent as relocation assistance, increased to three months for a senior or disabled tenant, through a direct payment within 15 days of notice or an equivalent rent waiver. The notice must explain the termination basis, assistance, and applicable reoffer rights; if the tenant fails to vacate when the notice expires, the landlord may recover assistance actually provided as damages in a possession action.

rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, under a lawful natural-person tenancy for continuous use or occupancy exceeding 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and their extensions or renewals of three months or less. The relocation entitlement concerns no-fault termination, regardless of income or length of a qualifying tenancy; the increased amount requires a tenant aged 62 or older or disabled as defined in Government Code section 12955.3. A government or court determination that the tenant is at fault for conditions triggering an order or need to vacate under section 98.0704(b)(3) removes section 98.0706(c) relocation entitlement. rules.exemptions: Use actual rent under the lease in effect on the notice date. Exclude every section 98.0703 circumstance: statutory transient/tourist hotels; locally defined short-term residential occupancy; document-restricted affordable housing for very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing other than Section 8 tenant-based assistance; Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious-facility, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care, adult residential-facility, and nonprofit transitional housing; institution-owned-and-operated higher-education or K–12 dormitories; bathroom/kitchen sharing with a principal-resident landlord; landlord-principal-residence single-family housing, including the specified no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and mobilehomes; a two-unit single structure with a landlord occupying one unit as a principal residence from tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; and separately alienable housing whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management and whose tenants received the prescribed written exemption notice, in the lease for commencement or renewal on or after January 1, 2024. Nonprofit transitional housing is nonprofit-operated temporary housing up to 24 months with supportive services aimed at permanent housing. The compensation threshold depends on the relocation assistance available to this tenant under section 98.0706(c), including the three-month amount for tenants aged 62 or older or disabled under Government Code section 12955.3 rather than the ordinary two-month amount, and any applicable section 98.0704(b)(3) government/court tenant-fault exclusion. These detailed exemptions and tenant-specific entitlement conditions require execution review.
rules.exemptions: Buyout agreements are landlord payments of money or other consideration for vacancy and exclude settlements of pending unlawful-detainer actions. Required bold statements cover the right not to agree, the right to consult an attorney, and invalidity of compensation below relocation assistance to which the tenant is entitled under federal, state, or local law. Translation is required if the tenant primarily negotiates either the buyout agreement or lease, orally or in writing, in a non-English language. The nonwaiver provision reaches a buyout agreement, lease, contract, or other agreement. The text requires compensation greater than section 98.0706(c) assistance but expressly declares amounts less than assistance owed void; the treatment of exact equality is reserved for review.
rules.quoted_span:
(c) Requirements for Buyout Agreements. The landlord shall comply with the 
following: 
(1) The buyout agreement shall be in writing. 
(2) A copy of the buyout agreement shall be given to each tenant at the 
time the tenant signs the buyout agreement. 
(3) The buyout agreement shall include the following statements in bold 
letters in at least 14-point font in close proximity to the space reserved 
for the signature of the tenant: 
(A) You, the tenant, have a right not to enter into this buyout 
agreement.  
Ch. Art. Div.  
9 8 7 18 
 
San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9:  Building, Housing and Sign Regulations   
(3-2024) 
 
 
 
(B) If you, the tenant, are entitled to relocation assistance under 
federal, state, or local law, a buyout agreement for less than the 
amount of the relocation assistance to which you are entitled 
violates Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 7 of the San Diego 
Municipal Code and is void. 
(C) You, the tenant, may choose to consult with an attorney before 
signing this agreement. 
(4) If the tenant primarily negotiates the buyout agreement or lease, orally 
or in writing, in a non-English language, the landlord shall provide the 
tenant with an English and a translated version of the buyout 
agreement at the same time. 
A buyout agreement that does not strictly comply with all the requirements of 
section 98.0707(c)(1)-(4) shall be void. 
(d) Void Buyout Agreements. Buyout agreements must be for an amount that is 
greater than the amount of relocation assistance available to the tenant in 
section 98.0706(c). A buyout agreement for less than the amount of relocation 
assistance owed to the tenant violates this Division and is void. 
(e) No Waiver. The provisions of section 98.0707 may not be waived by a buyout 
agreement. Any term of a buyout agreement, lease, contract, or other 
agreement which purports to waive or limit a tenant's rights under 
section 98.0707 is contrary to public policy, unenforceable, and void.

rules.title: Tenant remedies and invalid termination notices
rules.requirement: A tenant claiming a Division violation may sue the landlord for injunctive or equitable relief and damages including punitive damages, raise noncompliance as a possession-action defense, recover at least three times actual economic damages for attempted or completed unlawful recovery of possession, and recover not less than three times required relocation assistance and actual economic damages for failure to provide required relocation assistance. A landlord's noncompliance voids termination notices required by the Division; reasonable attorney fees and costs are discretionary for an attempt to recover possession in material violation, remedies are cumulative, and the City may enforce through the referenced civil and criminal remedies.
rules.key_value: Minimum treble-damage remedies for specified violations
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks, under a lawful natural-person tenancy for continuous use or occupancy exceeding 30 days, excluding fixed-term leases of three months or less and their extensions or renewals of three months or less. Exclude every section 98.0703 circumstance: statutory transient/tourist hotels; locally defined short-term residential occupancy; document-restricted affordable housing for very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households; qualifying subsidized affordable housing other than Section 8 tenant-based assistance; Mobilehome Residency Law mobilehomes; nonprofit hospital, religious-facility, extended-care, licensed elderly residential-care, adult residential-facility, and nonprofit transitional housing; institution-owned-and-operated higher-education or K–12 dormitories; bathroom/kitchen sharing with a principal-resident landlord; landlord-principal-residence single-family housing, including the specified no-more-than-two-bedroom, two-ADU, or two-JADU circumstances and mobilehomes; a two-unit single structure with a landlord occupying one unit as a principal residence from tenancy commencement and continuously thereafter; a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years unless the housing is a mobilehome; and separately alienable housing whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management and whose tenants received the prescribed written exemption notice, in the lease for commencement or renewal on or after January 1, 2024. Nonprofit transitional housing is nonprofit-operated temporary housing up to 24 months with supportive services aimed at permanent housing. Any underlying entitlement must also satisfy its tenant-specific conditions, including senior/disability status for enhanced relocation and the section 98.0704(b)(3) government/court tenant-fault exclusion from relocation. Exact exemptions and underlying entitlements require execution review. Coverage does not establish a violation, damages, liability, or entitlement to a particular remedy.
rules.exemptions: Tenant standing is stated for a tenant claiming a violation, in a court of competent jurisdiction. The wrongful-eviction minimum concerns attempted or actual recovery of possession in violation of the Division; the relocation remedy concerns failure to provide assistance required by section 98.0706(c); discretionary fees concern attempted recovery in material violation. The text does not specify per-violation counting or fixed civil/criminal penalties. Section 98.0709(e)'s wording is retained without resolving whether its multiplier reaches both relocation assistance and actual economic damages.
rules.quoted_span:
§98.0709 Remedies 
(a) A tenant claiming a violation of this Division may file an action against a 
landlord in a court of competent jurisdiction. 
 
(b) A tenant may seek injunctive relief, equitable relief, and money damages, 
including punitive damages, in a civil action against a landlord for a violation 
of this Division.  
Ch. Art. Div.  
9 8 7 19 
 
San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9:  Building, Housing and Sign Regulations   
(3-2024) 
 
 
 
(c) A tenant may raise, as an affirmative defense, any violation or noncompliance 
with this Division in any action by a landlord to recover possession of a 
residential rental property. 
 
(d) Any attempt by a landlord to recover possession of a residential rental 
property or any actual recovery of possession of a residential rental property 
in violation of this Division shall render the landlord liable to the tenant in a 
civil action for wrongful eviction for damages of not less than three times the 
actual economic damages. 
 
(e) Any landlord who fails to provide relocation assistance as required by 
section 98.0706(c) shall be liable to the tenant in a civil action for not less 
than three times the required relocation assistance and actual economic 
damages. 
 
(f) In the court's discretion, a landlord who attempts to recover possession of a 
residential rental property in material violation of this Division shall be liable 
to the tenant in a civil action for reasonable attorney’s fees and costs. 
 
(g) The remedies under section 98.0709 are cumulative and may be used in 
addition to any other remedies in this Division or at law, statute, or ordinance. 
 
(h) The City may enforce this Division under Chapter 1, Article 2 of this Code, 
including civil and criminal remedies. 
(“Remedies” added 5-25-2023 by O-21647 N.S.; effective 6-24-2023.) 
(Amended 2-27-2024 by O-21769 N.S.; effective 3-28-2024.) 
 
§98.0710 Failure to Comply with Division 
In addition to other remedies applicable to landlord’s failure to comply with this 
Division, a landlord’s failure to comply with any provision of this Division shall 
render void any notice of termination required by this Division.  
(“Failure to Comply with Division” added 2-27-2024 by O-21769 N.S.; effective 
3-28-2024.)

rules.title: Just cause required for covered tenancy terminations
rules.requirement: Landlords may terminate a tenancy covered by the JCO only for a qualifying just cause.
rules.key_value: Six months of occupancy or expiration of the original lease, whichever comes first
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City's RSO, once the tenant has occupied the same unit for at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first. The source identifies exceptions, expressly not exhaustive, for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. The qualifications for these exceptions require review. Buildings newer than October 1, 1978 and properties containing only one single-family dwelling can be covered.
rules.exemptions: The identified property and tenancy exceptions are preserved in coverage_conditions. Listed at-fault grounds are nonpayment of rent, failure to cure a rental-agreement violation, nuisance or property damage, illegal use, failure to renew a similar agreement, failure to provide reasonable access, and an unapproved subtenant remaining at lease end. Listed no-fault grounds are occupancy by the owner or an immediate family member; occupancy by a resident manager when required by law, an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement; demolition, permanent removal from the rental market or conversion to nonresidential use; a government order to vacate; HUD ownership and sale; residential hotel conversion or demolition; and conversion to affordable housing. The source does not establish the detailed prerequisites for each ground.
rules.citation: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance; LAHD guidance, Rental Units Covered Under JCO and Legal Reasons for Eviction
rules.quoted_span:
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
Just Cause Ordinance
(JCO).  It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.
Legal Reasons for Eviction
Tenant i
s at-fault
Under the JCO, the landlord may recover possession of a rental unit
in specific situations. Below is a list of reasons for which a tenant could be evicted and
would be considered at fault
. If the tenant is at fault
for the eviction, then the tenant will not be entitled to relocation assistance.
Failure to pay rent
Failure to cure a violation of the rental agreement
Creating a nuisance or causing damage to the property
Using the rental unit for an illegal purpose
Failure to renew a similar rental agreement
Failure to provide the landlord with reasonable access to the rental unit
The person at the end of the lease term is a subtenant not approved by the landlord
Tenant is not at-fault
Situations in which the property owner wishes to regain the use of the rental unit, as the result of a personal or business decision, and
not the
tenant’s fault, may be cause for eviction, but the property owner may have to pay the tenant
relocation assistance
. These reasons include
The
owner or an immediate family member
will move into the rental unit
Resident manager will move into the rental unit when required by law or by an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement
Demolition, permanent removal from the rental market, or conversion to
non-residential
Government order to vacate
HUD owns and is selling the property
Residential Hotel being converted or demolished
Conversion to affordable housing

rules.title: Relocation assistance for qualifying no-fault evictions
rules.requirement: Property owners must provide relocation assistance for no-fault evictions that qualify for assistance under the JCO. Tenants evicted for an at-fault reason are not entitled to that assistance.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in Los Angeles outside the City's RSO, after the tenant has lived in the same unit for at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first. Exceptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties; the source makes this list nonexhaustive and leaves several qualifications unspecified. Newer buildings and properties containing only one single-family dwelling can be covered. Any additional tenancy or property eligibility conditions for relocation assistance require review because the source says owners may have to pay without supplying those details.
rules.exemptions: At-fault evictions do not entitle the tenant to relocation assistance. Potential no-fault grounds listed are owner or immediate-family occupancy; resident-manager occupancy required by law, an affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement; demolition, permanent removal from the rental market or conversion to nonresidential use; a government order to vacate; HUD ownership and sale; residential hotel conversion or demolition; and conversion to affordable housing. The source does not specify payment amounts or establish that every listed no-fault eviction requires payment.

rules.title: Post and provide the Notice of Right to Counsel
rules.requirement: Landlords must post a Notice of Right to Counsel in a conspicuous common area of the residential building where the tenant resides. They must also provide it to the tenant at the beginning of the tenancy and whenever an eviction notice is served.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Required Registration and Posted Notification
rules.quoted_span:
Beginning August 20, 2025, landlords must post a
Notice of Right to Counsel
in a conspicuous common area of the residential building where the tenant resides. This notice is also to be provided to the tenant at the beginning of the tenancy and anytime an eviction notice is served.

rules.title: Provide and post the Notice of Renters’ Protections
rules.requirement: All landlords of residential properties must provide a Notice of Renters’ Protections to tenants who begin or renew their tenancy on or after January 27, 2023. Landlords must also post the notice in an accessible common area of the property.
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential rental properties in Los Angeles are within the stated posting scope; individual delivery is required for tenants whose tenancy begins or renews on or after January 27, 2023. The allowed facts cannot represent that tenancy commencement or renewal date.
rules.exemptions: The source states no exemption from this notice duty; the January 27, 2023 tenancy commencement or renewal condition applies to individual delivery.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Required Registration and Posted Notification
rules.quoted_span: All landlords of residential properties must provide a Notice of Renters’ Protections to tenants who begin or renew their tenancy on or after January 27, 2023. This notice must also be posted in an accessible common area of the property.

rules.title: Rent arrears must exceed Fair Market Rent for nonpayment eviction
rules.requirement: Landlords of RSO or JCO rental units may not evict a tenant for falling behind in rent unless the amount owed exceeds the Fair Market Rent applicable to the unit’s bedroom size.
rules.key_value: Rent owed must exceed bedroom-size Fair Market Rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units in Los Angeles covered by either the City's RSO or JCO. The source does not define RSO eligibility. For the JCO branch, the source describes residential properties outside the RSO and a tenant who has lived in the same unit for at least six months or whose original lease has expired, whichever occurs first; it also identifies nonexhaustive exceptions for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. Those exception qualifications and the RSO branch require review.
rules.exemptions: This is a restriction on nonpayment evictions, not a statement that exceeding the threshold independently authorizes eviction. The source provides no current bedroom-specific FMR amounts.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Evictions for Non-Payment of Rent
rules.quoted_span: Applies to all RSO & JCO rental units. Effective March 27, 2023, landlords may not evict a tenant who falls behind in rent unless the tenant owes an amount higher than the Fair Market Rent (FMR). The FMR depends on the bedroom size of the rental unit.

rules.title: File eviction notices with LAHD
rules.requirement: Landlords issuing eviction notices for JCO or RSO rental properties must file those notices with LAHD within three business days after service on the tenant.
rules.key_value: Three business days after service
rules.coverage_conditions: Los Angeles rental properties covered by the JCO or RSO. RSO coverage criteria are not supplied. The JCO scope described in this source is residential rental property outside the RSO, with tenant occupancy of at least six months or expiration of the original lease, whichever occurs first, and nonexhaustive exceptions for transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. Review is needed to establish the unspecified exception qualifications and whether the JCO tenancy waiting period also limits this property-level filing duty.
rules.exemptions: The passage expressly identifies JCO and RSO rental properties as its scope, despite subsequently referring to all eviction notices issued in the City.
rules.citation: LAHD JCO guidance, Eviction Notices Filed with LAHD
rules.quoted_span: Applies to all JCO & RSO rental properties – All eviction notices issued to tenants in the City of Los Angeles must be filed with LAHD within three (3) business days of service on the tenant.

review.quoted_span: The landlord shall be entitled to decontrol the apartment unit under this article only under the following circumstances:

review.issue: Section 155-30 is referenced but not supplied, and the capture contains Article VII rather than the whole chapter. Registration requirements and any chapter-wide definitions or exemptions cannot be fully resolved from this source.
review.quoted_span: Provided that a dwelling is registered in accordance with § 155-30 upon the vacation of a residential apartment unit by a tenant, the apartment unit shall become decontrolled and exempt from the provisions of this chapter for the new tenant's initial rental; provided, however, that said rental shall be limited to an increase of 25% over the last rental paid by the tenant who voluntarily vacated the rental unit, exclusive of any capital improvement surcharge that is a component of said last rental.

review.issue: Section 155-31 describes the 25% comparison using the rent of a tenant who voluntarily vacated, while § 155-32 also permits decontrol following legal eviction or qualifying court-ordered vacancy. The calculation after those other vacancy circumstances requires review; no broader cap calculation is inferred.
review.quoted_span: If the tenant vacates the apartment voluntarily without harassment, duress or unreasonable pressure from the landlord or his agents or if the tenant is legally evicted.

review.issue: The relationship between the legal-eviction ground in subsection A and the holdover exclusion attached to the court-order ground in subsection B requires review. The extraction preserves both provisions without determining precedence or a verified conflict.
review.quoted_span: If the tenant vacates the apartment as a result of a court order from a court of competent jurisdiction. This ground shall not be available to a landlord who receives a court order to dispossess a tenant based upon the tenant holding over and continuing in possession of the premises after the expiration of his term.

review.issue: The source makes subsequent increases subject to Chapter 155 but does not supply that chapter's ordinary increase formula or other adjustment provisions. No ordinary recurring rent cap is inferred.
review.quoted_span: However, any additional rental increase beyond the initial rental of the new tenant shall be subject to the provisions of this chapter.

review.issue: The extraction includes the stated rescission, rent reversion and prosecution remedy. Section 155-21 is not supplied, so no fine amount, additional sanction, private plaintiff standing or per-violation counting rule is inferred.
review.quoted_span: If the Board finds that a landlord is seeking to decontrol or has decontrolled an apartment unit and the tenant has vacated the unit under circumstances other than those set forth in this section, the Rent Board may rescind the decontrol of the apartment unit, and the rent shall revert to that rental on the apartment unit prior to the vacation of the apartment, and prosecute the landlord for violation of the chapter under § 155-21 .

Violations of the HSNA are investigated by the Office of Fair Housing and Equity
(FHE) and enforced by the Inspectional Services Department (ISD). ISD will issue a
ticket to your landlord if the required information is not provided to you and you
properly report the violation.
In order for ISD to issue a ticket, you will need to do the following: 

Housing Stability Notification Act 
Frequently Asked Questions for Tenants 
3 
1. Call FHE at 617-635-2500 and explain that you are calling to report a
violation of the new Housing Stability Notification Act. You can also call 311
and ask for FHE.
2. FHE may direct you to submit your information through an online intake
form available on FHE’s website: boston.gov/departments/fair-housing-
and-equity. If you are unable to use the online form, you may submit any
required documentation through the mail to the following address:
City of Boston 
Office of Fair Housing and Equity 
1 City Hall Square, Rm. 966 
Boston, MA 02201 
3. Provide FHE with written proof of your tenancy such as your lease, rent
receipts, or your name on a notice to quit or court complaint (other items
proving your tenancy may be accepted).
4. Provide FHE with a copy of the Notice to Quit or Court Complaint, as well as
your landlord or property manager’s contact information.

The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
On April 14, 2020, Berkeley City Council passed the Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance (BMC 13.106). An overview of the ordinance is available below. Please review the Ordinance for more specific details related to your property or tenancy.

review.issue: The substantive duties are supported, but exemption details are not supplied. review.quoted_span:
Exemptions
Please view the Ordinance on specific requirements for each exemption.
Lifetime sex offenders
Public housing/Section 8 properties limited exemptions
Owner-occupied properties (between 1-3 units) in which an owner of record resides in one of the units as their primary residence
Units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back to their home in accordance with BMC 13.76.130 A.9
Units occupied by existing tenant(s) seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates

review.issue: Separately located sanctions apply to any landlord found in violation of the Ordinance: administrative fines of $1,000–$10,000 per violation; civil damages including actual damages or three times one month's rent; punitive damages; attorneys' fees and costs; and injunctive relief. review.issue: The source identifies administrative complaint eligibility for applicants or tenants with criminal records who believe a housing provider violated their rights during application, leasing or tenancy, and for close family members in the described circumstances. review.quoted_span: Applicants or tenants with criminal records who believe their rights have been violated by a housing provider under the terms of the Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance during the application, leasing, or tenancy process can file a complaint. Filing a complaint is also an option if you are a close family member of someone with a criminal record and you believe they were prevented by a housing provider from being added to your household on the basis of their criminal record, or from obtaining their own housing, or facing other adverse action from a housing provider.

review.issue: Proposed section 3(a) refers to a violation of “this section,” although the substantive prohibitions appear in section 2. review.issue: The proposal also provides an election against enforcing predispute arbitration agreements and joint-action waivers in related cases filed under federal, tribal, state or local law. The election belongs to the person alleging the conduct or the named class or collective representative; section 3(c)'s “this section” reference requires review before linking this remedy conclusively to section 2.
review.quoted_span: (c) At the election of the person alleging conduct constituting a violation of this section, or the named representative of a class or in a collective action alleging such conduct, no predispute arbitration agreement or predispute joint-action waiver shall be valid or enforceable with respect to a case which is filed under federal, tribal or state or local law and relates to a violation of this chapter.

review.issue: The proposed arbitration remedy uses these definitions, which limit it to agreements concerning disputes that had not yet arisen when the agreements were made.
review.quoted_span:
“Predispute arbitration agreement”, an agreement to arbitrate a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.
“Predispute joint-action waiver”, an agreement, whether or not part of a predispute arbitration agreement, that would prohibit or waive the right of one of the parties to participate in a joint, class or collective action in a judicial, arbitral, administrative or other forum, concerning a dispute that has not yet arisen at the time of the making of the agreement.

review.issue: Proposed section 4 supplies a pleading standard for a civil action filed under chapter 93 while describing a violation of chapter 93A. Preserve this procedural provision for review rather than treating it as an independent housing eligibility condition or silently correcting its chapter references.

Section 4. In a civil action filed pursuant to the provisions of chapter 93, a complaint:
(i) plausibly pleads a violation of chapter 93A if the complaint contains factual allegations demonstrating that the existence of a contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce is among the realm of plausible possibilities; and
(ii) need not allege facts tending to exclude the possibility of independent action.

review.issue: Remedies are stated in a separate passage and are therefore recorded here rather than added to requirements whose quotations do not contain them. review.quoted_span: If, during the Commission’s investigation, the evidence is sufficient to show that discrimination may have occurred (Probable Cause), the Commission will attempt conciliation between the parties. The Commission has the authority to provide various remedies after hearing, including filing a criminal complaint in District Court, levying civil fines of up to $300 for each violation, filing a civil complaint in Superior Court seeking injunctive relief, and seeking an award of damages, expenses and other relief. If Probable Cause is found in a complaint filed under the Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance, either party may opt to remove the case for trial in the Massachusetts Superior Court or to the Attorney General’s Office for review and resolution.

(g) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for All Items” means the following:
(A) The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for All Items (CPI-U) for the metropolitan area in which the property is located, as published by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, which are as follows:

(iv) The CPI-U for the San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward metropolitan area covering the Counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco, and San Mateo.

(C) On or after January 1, 2021, if the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes a CPI-U index for one or more metropolitan areas not listed in subparagraph (A), that CPI-U index shall apply in those areas with respect to rent increases that take effect on or after August 1 of the calendar year in
which the 12-month change in that CPI-U, as described in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (3), is first published.
(2) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.

calendar year and April of the year before that.

Family trust means a revocable living trust or irrevocable trust in which the settlors 
and beneficiaries of the trust are persons who are related to each other as sibling, 
spouse, domestic partner, child (by blood or adoption), parent, grandparent, or 
grandchild (by blood or adoption). 
 
Landlord means an owner and any person, acting as principal or through an agent,
